On an overcast and misty Friday afternoon, what was once a symbol of downtown Gary’s hopes and dreams for a vibrant economic future was transformed into a slowly building pile of twisted steel, bronze and glass debris as demolition equipment methodically gnawed away at the Genesis Convention Center.

A five-man crew from McDonough Demolition watched a pair of back hoes strip away the west side of the building, the material clanking and thumping as it crashed to the ground inside a fenced off area along Adams Street.

Meanwhile, patrons entered the Gary Public Library across the street seemingly paying no mind to the demolition of a building that had long-since failed to deliver on its promise of a downtown revitalization.

Opened in 1981, the Genesis Center hosted a variety of live entertainment, conventions and region-wide events, including concerts by Whitney Houston and Prince, but the facility eventually became a steady drain on city resources.

Two former Genesis Center directors stole money from its coffers in 2017 and 2018, according to Post-Tribune archives. Both pleaded guilty to federal charges. Deborah Black had to pay $16,000 in restitution, while Victoria Wilson agreed to repay the city $12,000 in her plea deal.

The building closed for good in 2020, and vandals started to strip the building of its materials. Its final big event came in 2019 when it welcomed mourners at the funeral of five-term mayor Richard G. Hatcher whose administration built the Genesis Center.

In 2025, the city installed a $9,000 camera security system at the center.

With maintenance costs mounting, Gary Mayor Eddie Melton announced in April that the 45-year-old structure would be demolished along with the adjacent parking garage.

The City of Gary said that the convention center ran “deep deficits for years,” costing taxpayers $8 million “in operational shortfalls over five years alone,” accordingly to a news release. Gary-based Powers and Sons Construction estimated repairs and stabilization costs would exceed $10 million.

Tackling pervasive urban blight, the city is also targeting the demolition of the former Gordon’s Department Store complex, City Methodist Church and St. Mary’s Mercy Hospital.

“From the Genesis Center and Gordon’s to long-standing safety hazards like St. Mary’s Hospital and City Methodist, holding onto unsalvageable buildings has cost our taxpayers millions and stalled our progress,” Melton said in the news release.

A demolition date for the church hasn’t been scheduled, but city officials anticipate a beginning in late October or early November. The city expects complete demolition and site restoration by Aug. 24, 2027.

To spur a new chapter of economic revitalization, the University of Notre Dame School of Architecture is collaborating with Gary on a citywide redevelopment program. Incoming developments include a new public safety facility, mixed-use housing and commercial development, a new metro center and a central civic plaza.

At 5th Avenue and Broadway, the city plans to add 150 residential units, ground-floor retail, and a mini-grocer and dining options, complemented by 90 units at 504 Broadway. The plaza will be an open gathering corridor that connects the Lake County Courthouse and Hudson-Campbell Sports and Fitness Center, which will commemorate the cultural history of the Genesis Center site.

Jim Masters is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

Former Special Counsel Jack Smith seized the personal payroll data of a notable conservative organization as part of his Arctic Frost lawfare against President Donald Trump, according to a new bombshell report.

Independent reporter Catherine Herridge broke the news on Friday that Smith’s team acquired the information from the renowned Conservative Partnership Institute (CPI) as part of its expansive probe. The revelation was included in whistleblower disclosures reportedly obtained by Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa.

According to Herridge, the February 2023 financial data nabbed by Smith’s team “included CPI employees’ medical, dental, and vision insurance coverage, along with a CPI bank statement.” The former Fox and CBS reporter further noted how “the collection of CPI’s February 2023 payroll data appears to go beyond the scope” of Smith’s original mandate to probe events surrounding the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol demonstrations.

Speaking with The Federalist, CPI Vice President of Programs Rachel Bovard said she is “at a loss to explain why Jack Smith thought the details of [her] dental and vision plans were part of a grand political conspiracy against democracy.” Blasting Smith for using the federal government to “harass and falsely accuse innocent conservatives for years,” The Federalist senior tech columnist noted how “it’s unconscionable that this was done in the name of ‘justice.'”

“There was no pursuit of justice — there was only weaponizing the legal process to punish Joe Biden’s political enemies,” Bovard added.

Grassley’s office revealed last year how CPI was one of numerous conservative organizations targeted in Smith’s Arctic Frost probe. The previous disclosures showed how the Biden FBI filed subpoenas seeking these groups’ banking and communication records.

Such invasive requests specifically named CPI’s Mark Meadows and Cleta Mitchell. While Meadows served as Trump’s White House chief of staff during his first term, Mitchell serves as chair of the Election Integrity Network and advised Trump on his post-2020 election litigation in Georgia.

Additional records released that same week by the House Judiciary Committee showed that the FBI targeted CPI President and CEO Ed Corrigan as part of Arctic Frost. The release disclosed communications among FBI officials, who were discussing allegations from an unidentified individual about Corrigan. This included outlandish claims that Corrigan and Meadows “are engaging in willful criminal activity,” and that Corrigan “has [redacted] properties at which he wants to build up infrastructure to train people for civil war.”

Herridge’s reporting comes days after Grassley sent a memo to his Senate Judiciary colleagues revealing that Smith acquired the personal information of at least 639,000 Republican voters, donors, and supporters in his Arctic Frost conquest. Among the obtained information were Republicans’ names, addresses, credit card data, and more. Data on MAGA hat sales and purchases was also reportedly collected.

Fox News Digital speaks to voters in the progressive bastion of Portland, Maine about their views on socialism.

PORTLAND, Maine — Americans who were asked for their opinions of socialism by Fox News Digital offered sharply different interpretations of the ideology, with some embracing its promises of economic equality while others expressed strong reservations about government control over the means of production.

Fox News Digital took to the streets of Maine's largest city, a progressive bastion, to talk to residents about their definitions of socialism and how far they would be willing to go to embrace its ideals.

The topic of socialism has featured prominently in campaign coverage during this midterm election cycle, as candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) scored high-profile victories over more centrist rivals in a slew of Democratic primaries this year. DSA's outsized influence has been a driving force in the ballot box battle for the Democratic Party's ideological future.

LIBERAL HOTSPOT RESIDENTS CAN'T AGREE ON WHAT SOCIALISM MEANS

Demonstrators hold a Democratic Socialists of America banner ahead of a Rent Guidelines Board vote in New York on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

A new Fox News national poll indicates 32% of voters have a favorable view of socialism, with 64% seeing it in an unfavorable way. But the favorable rating matches an all-time high, first reached five years ago, since Fox News first began asking the question in 2019. And a September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans had a positive image of socialism, the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010.

Lewis, a retired Navy veteran, said socialism was a good thing because it "looks out for people's needs.... and it's not communism."

Socialism and communism both emphasize collective ownership of the means of production, such as factories, businesses and major industries. But socialism encompasses a range of approaches, including those that allow private enterprise, while communism traditionally envisions the abolition of private ownership of productive assets and, ultimately, a classless society.

CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS NATIONAL POLL

Lewis turned skeptical when Fox News Digital asked whether he would personally surrender private property to government or collective control.

"I guess. I hadn't really thought about socialism that way. I think about taking care of the needs of people, you know, things like... national health care, things like that," he answered. "I don't like government taking things away from you."

Nolan, who recently moved to Portland, told Fox News Digital "there's a lot of wealth imbalance in America right now, and we could benefit from some sort of leveling system."

He said socialism exists to help "people who aren't as, you know, benefiting in society."

Nolan added that "business owners should have their autonomy" and that "people deserve to earn their money."

"But there are a lot of really high-end... corporations that benefit so much... that really don't need that much wealth... there's so much exorbitant wealth at the top end that a lot of that could trickle down to people who are disadvantaged and don't have homes," Nolan stated.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Nola, another resident passing through Portland's Monument Square, said socialism's "a good thing. It means equity."

Asked about the takeover of businesses and means of production under socialism, Nola said she still "100%" supported socialism.

"I'm the daughter of a small business owner. I've seen how tough it is to run a small business in this country and how easy it is for corporations to just do whatever they want," she explained. "So if we gave actually back to small businesses and the government helped them out... and so much of the market that's privatized actually became public, I think... with how big the U.S. has gotten, it's only a good thing."

Ted disagreed.

"Socialism overall, I think it's a horrible idea," he emphasized. "If we can learn from history, anything from history, we see that it's gonna really give way too much power to the government institution. It's gonna... make things that are harmful overall for everyone... it's like it's dictatorship."

Ted argued that "socialism just impoverishes. Capitalism, the free market economy is a good thing."

He added that while "some people are very wealthy and very greedy," that overall capitalism "creates other wealth for other people."

The new Fox News poll found that 51% of voters had a favorable view of capitalism, compared with 32% who viewed socialism favorably. Another 46% had an unfavorable view of capitalism.

Image not from story. (Photo by COLE BURSTON/AFP via Getty Images)

An explosion rocked a Canadian military base Saturday, leaving multiple dead and dozens injured as flames spread beyond the installation and local hospitals were overwhelmed.

At least seven people were killed and dozens injured at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, according Global News, citing multiple military sources. Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty confirmed the resuling fatalities and injuries but did not release an official casualty count.

“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” McGuinty told reporters Saturday, according to The Associated Press.

A fire broke out inside the base’s training area around 4 p.m. local time (6 p.m. EDT) Saturday before spreading beyond its boundaries, the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) confirmed in a statement.

Multiple military sources told Global News that a live-fire exercise struck a natural gas line or well, triggering an explosion and fire. Canadian military authorities, however, have not publicly confirmed that account at the time of writing.

An explosion and fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright east of Edmonton have resulted in an unknown number of fatalities and injuries, Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty says.Asked if there has been any similar incident at a military base, the minister said, “I cannot… pic.twitter.com/mlOJrfBZAE

Hospitals in Edmonton activated Code Orange mass-casualty protocols as patients were transferred from overwhelmed medical facilities in Wainwright, according to CBC News.

“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency physician at Royal Alexandra Hospital, told the outlet. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now.”

Ambulances also converged on Wainwright High School, which was reportedly used as an emergency staging area, according to local eyewitness accounts. Authorities have not, at the time of writing, confirmed whether patients were treated inside the building.

Acute Care Alberta confirmed emergency medical services were providing care and transportation, while Shock Trauma Air Rescue Service (STARS) Air Ambulance dispatched crews from Edmonton and Saskatoon.

Wind gusts reportedly reached 100 kilometers per hour (~62.1 mph) as flames crossed the military base’s perimeter fence, prompting firefighters from multiple jurisdictions to respond.

The Canadian Armed Forces said its immediate priority was supporting those affected and notifying next of kin, adding that official casualty figures would not be released until the notification process was complete.

Canada’s Department of National Defence did not confirm whether natural gas infrastructure or military fuel supplies were involved when contacted by the Daily Caller News Foundation.

“We are aware of an incident in Wainwright, Alberta. The safety and security of our personnel, their families, and members of the surrounding community remain our highest priority,” Suzanne Lalande, a representative of the department’s media relations office, told the DCNF in an emailed statement. “We are closely monitoring the situation and will provide additional information as it becomes available and can be confirmed.”

The Canadian military and Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating the incident, Defense Minister David McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa, according to Reuters.

The reported explosion sparked questions over whether natural gas infrastructure or military fuel supplies were involved. Before official confirmation, social media users — with some claiming personal familiarity with the installation or area — began sharing their thoughts and debating reports.

“This could be one of the biggest Canadian mass casualty events,” the @WogPogReal account said during a live X Space discussion the user hosted Saturday, predicting that the death toll could reach double digits.

The possibility of an oil or natural gas well explosion drew skepticism from participants who argued that flames from a well fire would rise vertically rather than spread predominantly in one direction, including user @CanadaPlus3. The direction of the flames alone, however, does not establish the fire’s cause.

The DCNF contacted Phoenix Gas to determine whether its natural gas infrastructure sustained damage. A company representative acknowledged the inquiry and indicated that the company would respond.

Another X Space participant, @jimmyjohn010, expressed a belief that military personnel were conducting a live-fire exercise when strong winds rapidly developed, potentially affecting operations on the firing range

Potential court-martial proceedings over alleged safety violations were also raised by user @jimmyjohn010, although Canadian authorities have not, at the time of writing, announced disciplinary action or determined whether military protocols were violated.

A forward fuel point, where military personnel store or distribute fuel during operations, was another possible source of the explosion suggested by X Space participants who identified themselves as former service members. Authorities, at the time of writing, have not confirmed a military fuel supply point was involved.

The possibility that incendiary munitions, including napalm, contributed to the explosion was also raised by X user @SamSteeleT89C.

“I felt/heard the boom but it was a good distance from me,” local resident Julie Verheul Tupling wrote on Facebook.

���Countless ambulances are staging at Wainwright High School from all over,” Tupling added, describing the emergency response.

Screenshot Julie Verheul Tupling’s Facebook Post

“I’ve done wireline work on that base.. there’s lots of oil wells below ground level, out in the field,” Rick Verheul, who identified himself as a former worker at the installation, wrote in a Facebook comment.

Some wellheads were situated approximately 10 to 15 feet below ground level, while workers were required to complete safety training before entering the military range, according to Verheul.

“We had to take a course before we went out on the range…what to do if we found a live round,” Verheul wrote, recalling an instance in which workers encountered ammunition that was subsequently removed.

The reported presence of oil and natural gas infrastructure at CFB Wainwright, however, does not establish whether those facilities were involved in Saturday’s explosion.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as serious, saying federal authorities were coordinating with provincial and municipal governments.

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” Carney wrote on X.

The Canadian Armed Forces, the Department of National Defence, and federal public safety officials were coordinating with Alberta and municipal authorities to mobilize emergency resources, according to McGuinty.

“My thoughts are with the families and with everyone impacted by this tragic event,” the minister said in an official statement which also thanked first responders and military personnel for their work.

“This is a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian Armed Forces,” General Jennie Carignan, Canada’s chief of the defense staff, added.

Carignan said military officials were prioritizing support for affected personnel and their families as casualty identification and next-of-kin notifications continued.

“Our soldiers, civilian personnel, and emergency responders are working closely with local authorities to respond to this situation,” Lieutenant-General Michael Wright, commander of the Canadian Army, stated.

Wright also expressed condolences to the families of those killed and pledged continued military assistance to those affected.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the incident “significant and tragic,” while Canadian lawmaker Dane Lloyd reported hearing of significant casualties.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training installations, hosting exercises for Canadian Armed Forces personnel. It houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre.

The cause of the incident remains under investigation.

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

grocery-store-wedding-cakes:
By

Stephan Bisaha

A flight of wedding cake samples at a Publix supermarket in Vestavia Hills, Ala., on Sept. 23. Cake flavors from left to right are red velvet, carrot cake, chocolate and vanilla. Filling flavors from left to right are raspberry, vanilla custard, cookies-and-cream mousse and strawberry.
                
                    
                    Stephan Bisaha
                    
                
                hide caption

Going to a specialty baker to craft your dream wedding cake can cost you more than $1,000.

Or you can order a few half sheet cakes from Costco for about $30 each.

"We love Costco, first of all," said Anna Holleran, who got married in California's Bay Area this year — and, yes, picked up her wedding cake from the grocery wholesaler.

"Their cakes are so good," she said. "How can you go wrong?"

Weddings are one of the most expensive days in many people's lives, costing on average about $36,000, according to the wedding-planning website Zola. The Bank of America Institute reports wedding spending among its customers was up 8.5% in May from a year earlier.

Some of that is by choice, with couples deciding to splurge on the venue or chasing the latest TikTok reception trend. But there are less controllable economic factors too, from inflation driving up the price of suits and catering to tariffs bumping up the cost of imported flowers and bridal gowns.

And according to Emily Forrest, head of communications at Zola, one place where couples are willing to trim costs is the cake. About a third of couples surveyed by Zola said they'd consider spending less on cake and dessert.

"When it comes to a wedding, every couple always has to sit down and say, 'Where are we going to save, and where are we going to splurge?'" said Forrest. "And cakes just don't seem to rise to the splurge occasion for a lot of couples."

What couples aren't willing to do is ditch the cake tradition entirely.

"You can't skip the cake!" said Lily Alana Stewart, who got married last year in central Alabama. "Everybody looks forward to a cake at a wedding."

To save money, she ordered her cake from Publix, a grocery chain in the South.

Stewart used baby's breath for decorating the venue, and Publix incorporated that into the cake design. Her co-workers who attended were surprised to learn where the cake came from. "They said, 'Wait, wait, wait. Your wedding cake was from Publix?'" Stewart said. "And they were still mind blown."

While the average wedding cake costs about $5.50 a slice, according to Zola, a slice of Publix cake is about $1.50 cheaper, while still pulling off that classic three-tiered, white-frosted wedding cake look. The chain also offers couples a tasting flight, so they can sample four flavors — including red velvet and carrot — before they order.

The wedding cake business has grown at Publix. The stores around Birmingham, Ala., sell about 50% more than they did before 2020, according to Jeff Brancato, a Publix retail improvement specialist. A chocolate cake with fondant that can serve 94 people costs $388, according to the price guide for the Birmingham area.

"There is definitely big savings when it comes to it," Brancato said.

Still, you do get what you pay for in a grocery store cake, including fewer options than what a specialty baker might offer — like more flavors or more customized decorations. While Publix touts its wedding cake business, Costco doesn't even list its half sheet as a wedding cake. It works out to about 70 cents per slice. (Costco did not return NPR's request for an interview.)

Holleran's priority was saving money where she could. Her wedding was near her home in California wine country — a region that's a destination spot for other couples and where venues are expensive.

Holleran said the culinary details of her cake weren't what mattered. "The real point is that you're sharing a dessert for the first time with somebody that you love," she said. "It's kind of symbolic of all the sweet moments that you're supposed to share in a marriage."

The roots of Russia's invasion of Ukraine go back decades and run deep. The current conflict is more than one country fighting to take over another; it is — in the words of one U.S. official — a shift in "the world order."Here are some helpful stories to make sense of it all.

By

The Associated Press

A policeman helps an elderly woman to walk out from a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.
                
                    
                    Kateryna Klochko/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.

The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating assaults with winter approaching.

Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities.

In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate, but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.

"A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote.

Later, in audio clips answering journalists' questions, Zelenskyy thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the legislation and praised its bipartisan support. He said blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and do nothing to bring the war to an end.

He also added that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate against Russian attacks would not bring peace.

"Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said.

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation.

The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.

Rescue workers walk in front of a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.
                
                    
                    Kateryna Klochko/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."

"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.

Zelenskyy also said Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.

"The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said.

Ukraine's air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.

A car burns after a Russian airstrike on a residential neighborhood in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday.
                
                    
                    Kateryna Klochko/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.

Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. Writing on social media, Liakh said that two apartment blocks were partially destroyed and other homes damaged.

A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine's Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said.

Elsewhere, a Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces had shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the Russian capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow's airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.

The Kremlin announced Saturday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.

Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Amazon has vowed to close more than a dozen warehouses and shed thousands of workers across New York City over a labor bill being pushed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani — and the e-commerce giant is likely to make good on the threat if the controversial legislation is enacted, industry experts told The Post.

The Delivery Protection Act would force Amazon to directly hire upwards of 5,000 delivery workers citywide who are currently employed by third-party contractors. Proponents say the legislation will increase workers’ pay and improve safety conditions at Amazon and other delivery firms including FedEx and DoorDash.

But Amazon doesn’t directly employ delivery workers anywhere else in the country — and has a history of fiercely resisting efforts to change its policies in the US and abroad. The result, according to experts, could be not only that those 5,000 delivery jobs move out of the city, but also that Amazon shutters its 15 last-mile warehouses in the Big Apple and fires the additional 2,000 workers that staff them.

Early last year, Amazon closed seven warehouses in Quebec near Montreal amid a labor fight involving one of its last-mile facilities. The union, Confédération des syndicats nationaux (CSN), had organized the 300 workers at a warehouse in the town of Laval.

By March 2025, some 1,900 Canadians across seven warehouses and 2,800 delivery contractors for those facilities had lost their jobs.

“Amazon will retaliate, because it has to send a firm message to the rest of the country that ‘If you mess with us, this is what will happen,’” said Marc Wulfraat, president and founder of Montreal-based logistics consulting firm, MWPVL International.

“When you look at Amazon’s global operations, they close buildings left, right and center when there is union activity.”

According to real estate listings, the Montreal facilities are now vacant, with Amazon still paying rent on more than 1.6 million square feet of space that it spent hundreds of millions of dollars to build, according to Wulfraat. At least two facilities are being offered as subleases.

The Delivery Protection Act — first introduced a year ago by Queens Council Member Tiffany Cabán and reintroduced in 2026 — has strong support in the City Council with some 34 co-signers. But several, including Speaker Julie Menin, are “uncomfortable” with potential job losses, a source close to negotiations said.

“This bill will have to pass in some form,” particularly since the mayor supports it, the source told The Post, adding that the final result may make “both sides unhappy.”

Compromises that have been discussed include allowing independent contractors to continue to perform deliveries while requiring Amazon to provide more safety guarantees for workers, the source said. No vote has been scheduled.

Industry experts say parallels between Quebec and New York can’t be ignored, even as Amazon employs directly or indirectly more than 12,000 hourly workers in New York — more than twice as many as it did in Quebec.

Those include the 2,000 workers that staff last-mile warehouses and 5,000 more to deliver the goods. The Delivery Protection Act wouldn’t affect 5,500 workers at Amazon’s giant JFK8 fulfillment center on Staten Island, who voted to unionize in 2022 — a first at an Amazon US facility — but who still lack a collective bargaining agreement.

While Amazon employs unionized workers in Europe, it has made headlines since the pandemic battling unions in the US. It’s now locked in litigation over allegedly hardball tactics it has used to fight labor organization in Bessemer, Ala., and Staten Island.

In April, the National Labor Relations Board ordered Amazon to the bargaining table with the Teamsters in Staten Island, but Amazon has filed lawsuits questioning the legitimacy of the NLRB.

“Amazon will say or do whatever it takes to deny workers stronger rights and wages and abdicate its responsibilities for its own employees,” the Teamsters said in a statement.

The risks posed by the Delivery Protection Act are not lost on the 40 independent companies that employ the 5,000 delivery workers in New York City.

“Look at what happened in Quebec,” Kris Basmagy, owner of DashWave Delivery, which handles Amazon’s deliveries on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, told The Post. “There was pressure on Amazon’s model, and it pulled out.”

Basmagy, who employs 150 delivery workers, added that nothing is stopping Amazon from replacing its New York City facilities with some of the “warehouses being built along the New Jersey Turnpike.”

Amazon is still tied up in litigation in Quebec, where it denies that it closed its warehouses because of CSN’s organizing activity. The union filed a complaint with Quebec’s labor tribunal, but even if it proves that Amazon violated labor laws, Amazon faces at most a fine and potential consumer backlash, according to a CBC News report.

A class action lawsuit filed by an Amazon Prime customer in Quebec in February 2025 claims that the warehouse closures slowed Amazon’s delivery times beyond the one- and two-day guarantee for Prime service — with some deliveries instead taking as long as four to six days.

In May, a Quebec court ruled that the case can proceed. Still, plaintiffs who are seeking refunds admit the disruption only lasted about two months, according to the complaint. Amazon says service hasn’t suffered since a large Canadian logistics company, IntelCom, took over its Quebec deliveries.

“Then they got their act together and stopped the delays,” said Saro Turner, a partner in the law firm Slater Vecchio, which filed the suit.

In New York, Amazon maintains that delivery times and prices for customers would increase if it closed its warehouses. New York is “fundamentally different” from Quebec, where Amazon operated “far fewer sites,” according to Amazon spokesperson Steve Kelly.

The company bankrolled a study by AKFR showing that the Delivery Protection Act would cost New Yorkers an extra $664 extra a year — or about $5.20 per package. That figure covers deliveries made by other companies, including FedEx and Doordash.

“New York City is one of the largest and most complex delivery regions in the country,” Kelly said in a statement. “It’s best served by a network of local small businesses deeply embedded in their communities and leveraging our operations infrastructure.”

Amazon deliveries in New York would slow permanently if it closed its last-mile facilities in the city, according to a source with knowledge of Amazon’s operations. Same-day deliveries and those that occur within hours of placing an order would take the biggest hit. The number of items that fall under the Prime promise would also shrink, this source said.

“There are a lot of same-day and same-morning deliveries in the city” that could arrive the next day, the source said.

Amazon’s last-mile facilities in Brooklyn and Queens include one in Red Hook at 270 Richards St. and another in Maspeth at 55-15 Grand Ave. Last-mile warehouses in Manhattan include an 87,000-square-foot facility at 706 11th Ave., according to a report on safety issues from New York City Comptroller Mark Levine.

“Amazon wouldn’t blink about shutting down the 15 facilities in New York City if it felt that the legislation was a threat to its business model,” said Brittain Ladd, a logistics and retail consultant and former Amazon executive. “This is about a model that could be copied in other cities.”

The delivery companies say they are the collateral damage in this struggle.

“There is a laser focus on punishing Amazon no matter what the repercussions might be, what it does to us as business owners, fathers and husbands,” Basmagy said. “It’s as if we no longer exist.”

WGA Transit, which has actively recruited formerly incarcerated and homeless workers to deliver Amazon packages in Harlem, will be forced out of business if the Delivery Protection Act is enacted in its current form, owner Joe Artus told The Post.

“I have a 21-month-old daughter,” Artus told The Post. “If this thing passes, there is no way for my company to exist or to keep my 189 employees.”

largest-private-conservation-bison-1000:
As autumn descends upon the Great Plains of North America, the largest private land conservation project in the country is ringing in an inspirational milestone.

The resident herd of relatively free-roaming bison now numbers 4 digits for the first time since the organization’s founding more than 20 years ago.

American Prairie is a conservation nonprofit that GNN readers may be familiar with. The group is quite simply attempting to stitch together the largest contiguously-wild stretch of North American Prairie in the country for the purpose of conservation and recreation.

Stitching together grasslands, water features, ranchland, rolling hills, and woodland, the reserve has accumulated 603,657 acres, which comprises 167,070 deeded acres and 436,587 leased public acres. The goal is ultimately to protect and some cases rewild 3.2 million acres—far harder to achieve for citizens than government lawmakers.

Yet in the over 20 years that American Prairie has been working, they’ve expanded their reserve to such an extent that if it were declared a National Park, it would rank among the nation’s 10 largest across the Lower 48.

Americans know that tens of millions of bison used to roam the prairie, and that those herds were almost wiped out long ago. What most Americans won’t know is why they haven’t returned yet.

Today, bison may number as little as 1 to 3.5% of their pre-industrial numbers. Of that total, less than 10% are managed for conservation or as a wild species. American Prairie details that most conservation herds are very small and are mostly confined to small, fenced-in areas. These conditions threaten the genetic health of bison and greatly hinder their ability to roam widely, display natural behaviors, and impart their ecological impact—so necessary to the flourishing of the prairie—onto the landscape.

Some of the chief hurdles to bison restoration are legal ones. Montana, where most of American Prairie’s acres area located, classify bison as livestock, not wildlife. As such, their movements and grazing are regulated the way cattle are—through a system meant to prevent cross-breeding, disease spreading, and encroachment.

MORE FROM THE PRAIRIE: Land Was Owned by Billionaires Who Didn’t Allow Access to National Monument – Now it’s Open

American Prairie recently had to take to the courts to defend its bison herd. On September 4th, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction to block the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) from enforcing its order requiring American Prairie to remove its bison from 3 federal grazing allotments in northeastern Montana.

BLM revoked American Prairie’s bison grazing permits in May 2026, and ordered the nonprofit organization to remove its bison from federal public lands, which make up the majority of the reserve. The order was made under an interpretation of a federal grazing rights law which the BLM saw as providing land solely for the commercial production of food and fiber.

American Prairie’s interpretation, which the judge said seemed highly likely to be correct, was that the Taylor Grazing Act includes no such distinction between commercial purposes and other purposes, such as conservation or recreation.

MORE FROM THIS NONPROFIT: 100 Miles of Derelict Fencing Removed by Rewilders Across the Great Plains in Montana

Fresh off of this intermittent legal victory, American Prairie’s annual calf count coming at the end of the breeding season put the size of the nonprofit’s herd at 1,016, the first time it’s ever held a thousand-handle.

Organizers believe a herd of 5,000 is a very achievable aim, but 5,000 square miles—the ultimate size they hope their land package reaches—would in theory provide suitable space for tens of thousands of bison.

In this article

Nvidia's Jensen Huang draws a crowd wherever he goes.

In an old converted church in West London on Wednesday night, Huang stood on a pop-up stage in front of politicians, investors, tech execs and journalists, announcing the chip giant was taking stakes in five U.K. startups.

"We're not your largest investor, but we are your best investor," he proclaimed. "I'm gonna invest in you, I'm gonna invest in you," he shouted, pointing at the founders. His appearance in London was part of a European tour ahead of Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin next week.

Earlier, he'd searched out U.K. neocloud Nscale CEO Josh Payne in the crowd, declaring, "last year you were zero."

"Now look at them," he said. "We invested in you, I attracted a whole bunch of investors to you." Nscale could be the most valuable British company in a decade, Huang said to cheers from the crowd.

The Nvidia boss certainly doesn't lack for confidence.

The warm reception Huang regularly receives is a sign of just how much sway he holds in the AI industry.

Nvidia has a near monopoly over the most powerful AI chips and Huang courts tech execs and world leaders with ease. He's a near constant presence at U.S. President Donald Trump's side at state dinners and visits.

In London, after the pomp and ceremony of Huang's speech, he emerged around 40 minutes late to a media huddle outside the front of the church.

"The Prime Minister [Andy Burnham] and I had a nice whiskey together. He's a whiskey man," he told reporters. Later, Huang said he'd be meeting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz "in a couple of days."

Huang spoke to journalists for nearly an hour that evening — a fair effort considering he'd only eaten a "quarter of a quarter" of a sandwich that day — dishing out praise and criticism to Europe with a bombastic assuredness.

"Nothing pains me more, frankly, than to see one of the most technologically advanced countries to be left so far behind in technology," he said, referring to Germany.

And the U.K. didn't escape scot-free. "If you tell an entrepreneur there's one in a million chance they can succeed, that entrepreneur says, 'So you're telling me there's a chance?' But in the UK, somehow there's 999,000... reasons to fail."

The CEO was also bullish on Europe's chances of succeeding with AI, not least, presumably, because Nvidia now has stakes in so many of the region's most promising startups.

On Wednesday those lucky startups were biotechs Prima Mente and Boltz, project delivery platform Foresight, algorithm discovery startup Hiverge and quantum company Riverlane. Those companies, alongside others in the U.K. that Nvidia isn't naming, will be the recipients of $1.16 billion of Nvidia cash.

Earlier in the week the chip giant announced it was taking stakes in a number of French startups.

It's all part of a major push by Nvidia to build out holdings across the AI stack. Among the recipients of funding from Nvidia have been the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI.

The chip giant has participated in 116 investment rounds in 2026 so far, according to Dealroom, up from just 12 in 2022.

Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO, according to people familiar with the matter.

By WILL POTTER, US SENIOR NEWS REPORTER

Published:  05:37 AEDT, 16 October 2026   |  Updated:  06:57 AEDT, 16 October 2026

A Texas woman who killed a college student in a drunken crash has been sentenced to seven years in prison, after which she will be forced to return to jail on Christmas and the birthdays of her victims for the following decade.

Lynlee Pollis, 30, killed Southern Methodist University student Honor Wallace, 19, and severely injured her friend Catherine 'CeCe' Solberg, 21, in a senseless car wreck in Dallas, Texas, in September 2023.

She was convicted earlier this month on intoxication manslaughter and intoxication assault charges, and sentenced to seven years in prison plus 10 years' probation.

After her release, Pollis will also serve an additional 15 days in jail each year of her probation, including her victims' birthdays, her own birthday, at Christmas, and the date of the crash.

The parents of Wallace and Solberg condemned Pollis at her sentencing hearing for putting their families through a grueling two-week trial, saying she could have spared them with a guilty plea.

'You were so drunk, and you wouldn't admit it,' Solberg's father Bobby told the court, per the Dallas Morning News.

'You made us sit through this trial... We've seen no personal accountability from you.'

Wallace's father said in his victim impact statement: 'You took the most precious gift from us through your selfishness. Own it. Own what you did.'

Lynlee Pollis, 30, who killed a college student in a drunken crash, has been sentenced to seven years in prison followed by returns to jail on the birthdays of her victims

The crash in September 2023 killed Southern Methodist University student Honor Wallace, 19, and severely injured her friend

Pollis was led out of the courtroom in handcuffs after the sentencing hearing, and she was reportedly seen mouthing 'I love you' to her family as she was escorted to jail.

Police said the crash that killed Wallace came when Pollis slammed into her car as she drove through a green light at an intersection.

Pollis was traveling 67mph in a 35mph zone at the time, and had run a red light that had changed over five seconds beforehand when she collided with Wallace's vehicle.

Wallace suffered fatal injuries and was pronounced dead at hospital, while Solberg, who was in the passenger seat, was diagnosed with severe brain trauma.

Solberg testified at the trial that she continues to suffer side effects from her injuries, including debilitating migraines.

Prosecutors said Pollis had been drinking a significant amount of alcohol before she drove on the day of the crash, and her blood alcohol levels were found to be 0.294% – almost four times the legal limit.

'This was no accident. This was no mistake,' prosecutor Andrew James said in his closing argument.

'It was predictable consequences of the defendant’s choices.'

Honor Wallace's father described her as a 'precious gift'

Pollis's attorneys had requested she be sentenced to only probation because she had no prior criminal record, but James said such a sentence would be 'completely inappropriate' given the circumstances of the crash.

Friends of the victims laid into Pollis at her sentencing hearing, with Haley Keller saying she is still haunted by the sight of Solberg in hospital covered in Wallace's blood.

'I couldn’t get the sight of all that blood out of my mind,' Keller said. 'Wherever I looked I saw Honor’s blood all over CeCe.'

Pollis's father said his daughter had been filled with regret every day since the crash, and said she was on suicide watch for days after the incident as she wished she was the one who died.

A Perth woman has been charged after allegedly putting poisonous snail pellets in a colleague's curry in an apparent attempt to poison her.

Police said the incident happened in February at a workplace in Oldbury, a semi-rural area south-east of Perth.

They said the alleged victim, a 58-year-old woman, brought a container of curry to work to share with colleagues.

During a morning tea break, the curry was shared among employees and eaten without issue.

But at lunchtime, the woman went back to eat more of the curry and noticed bright green granules in the food.

After tasting it, she reported experiencing numbness to her tongue.

The food was kept and was given to police.

Police allege between morning tea and lunch, a 43-year old woman accessed a chemical storage shed, then went back to the staff room where the food was kept and allegedly added snail pellets to the curry.

They have charged her with one count of endangering the life, health or safety of a person.

Police say the two women were also in a "personal relationship" together.

An investigation by detectives allegedly identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.

She is due to appear in Armadale Magistrates Court on November 5.

This week’s round-up of business news from the UK railway industry from Rail Business UK.

Stockport Council and Transport for Greater Manchester have launched a public consultation on a transformation of Stockport station as part of a wider programme of investment in the town. This aims to improve accessibility, connectivity and the overall station environment while supporting wider regeneration and investment across Stockport.

Newcastle-based Full Circle Brew Co has created a beer named Brewmo for sale on Lumo’s East Coast Main Line services. ‘We’re extremely proud that one of our craft beers will be served exclusively on local rail services. We’re confident that Brewmo will be just the ticket for Lumo’s customers’, said Ben Cleary, who founded Full Circle Brew Co in 2019. Its beers are now sold across the UK and exported to 12 countries.

More than 350 rail workers went to Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale for rail contractor QTS Group’s first Safety Jamboree. A total of 18 suppliers and exhibitors supported the two-day event, including Eave, Altrad Belle, Garic, Speedy, Instagrid, Rock Fall Boots, ATG Gloves, Signal PPE, Eurosafe which provided a confined space training simulator, Milwaukee, Flannery Plant Hire which brought an excavator simulator, Ritelite, Select Group, Hirst Bros, Rope Access Solutions and Tree Heroes. DAGS Services donated 10 benches, which were used during the event and will stay at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp.

Severfield Structural Solutions has been appointed to Network Rail’s £70m steel piles framework, supporting the delivery of overhead line equipment across the network. The six-year contracts start in January 2027, with a possible two-year extension. The appointment draws on the specialist expertise of DAM Structures, which became part of Severfield Group in 2021. ‘This is an important win for Severfield and reflects the strength of our engineering capabilities and the expertise of our teams’, said CEO Paul McNerney. ‘Our refreshed strategy is focused on building on what we do best, deepening customer relationships and pursuing opportunities in markets where we have a strong track record.’

East West Railway Co has dropped plans to build a Cambridge Eastern Train Care Centre at Fulbourn in Cambridgeshire. Train care and stabling facilities will now be provided at a combination of existing rail industry-owned sites elsewhere in the Eastern region, none of which are in Cambridgeshire.

texas-border-drug-seizure-2026:
In the span of less than a week, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers managed to derail the plans of two drug couriers to bring $657,000 in narcotics into the United States through a single port of entry. Two United States citizens are now facing criminal charges for their roles in the failed smuggling venture at the Del Rio, Texas, Port of Entry.

The first of the two failed drug smuggling events unfolded on October 8, when a man driving a 2013 GMC Acadia sought entry into the United States from Mexico at the Del Rio International Bridge. A CBP Office of Field Operations officer referred the driver and vehicle to a secondary inspection area for a thorough inspection.

During the inspection process, officers examined the vehicle using non-intrusive technology. Based on the scan results, officers conducted a physical search and found 16 packages of suspected contraband hidden in the vehicle. Officers examined the packages and found they contained a total of 23.68 pounds of a substance believed to be cocaine. Officials said the contraband has an estimated street value of $316,142.

CBP officers seized the narcotics and referred the case to ICE Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) special agents, who arrested the driver, a 23-year-old United States citizen. A criminal investigation of the incident is underway.

On Sunday, officers at the same port of entry thwarted another smuggling attempt when a man attempted to enter the United States from Mexico while driving a 2005 Ford Expedition. After an initial interview, officers referred the driver and vehicle to a secondary inspection area for a more detailed search. Officers conducted a secondary examination of the vehicle using a non-intrusive inspection system.

After conducting a physical search based on the results of the scan, officers located 30 packages containing a total of 37.08 pounds of a substance believed to be methamphetamine hidden under the spare tire of the vehicle. The street value of the contraband is estimated to be $340,975.

CBP officers seized the contraband and referred the case to the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS). The driver was placed under arrest by DPS investigators and now faces prosecution under the Texas Controlled Substances Act.

Del Rio Port of Entry Acting Port Director Julian DeHoyos commented on the seizures, saying, “In just four days, exceptional target profiling and rigorous inspections led to these significant seizures. This string of successful actions underscores our absolute commitment to dismantling the networks trying to poison our communities.”

The Del Rio Port of Entry is one of ten southwest border ports of entry that fall under the purview of the Laredo Field Office. As reported by Breitbart Texas, the region is the second busiest in the nation for narcotics seizures by CBP. The region stretches from Del Rio, Texas, on the north end and runs 450 miles south through Laredo and onward to Brownsville, the southern tip of Texas.

Randy Clark is a 32-year veteran of the United States Border Patrol.  Before his retirement, he served as the Division Chief for Law Enforcement Operations, directing operations for nine Border Patrol Stations within the Del Rio, Texas, Sector. Follow him on X (formerly Twitter) @RandyClarkBBTX.

‘The Five’ discuss a report saying former Vice President Kamala Harris’ husband, Doug Emhoff, does not want her to run for president again and what it could mean for her political future.

As former Vice President Kamala Harris weighs another White House run in 2028, a longtime advisor is firing back at Democratic strategists and donors who argue she has squandered an opportunity to politically reinvent herself following her 2024 election defeat.

Veteran Democratic strategist Maria Cardona, an outside advisor to Harris, pushed back against the criticism highlighted in a new Politico report, defending Harris' policy proposals and campaign activity as Democrats debate whether the former vice president deserves another shot at the White House. Cardona argued the story was "infuriating in its silliness."

The report, based on interviews with nearly 20 California-based Democratic donors and strategists, highlighted growing skepticism among some party insiders about Harris' political future and whether she has done enough to distinguish herself from her unsuccessful 2024 campaign.

Longtime Democratic strategist Doug Herman, a veteran of former President Barack Obama’s 2008 and 2012 campaigns, told Politico that Harris "totally blew it ... She hasn’t gotten into the mix."

AOC GIVES MAJOR HINT ABOUT 2028

Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks during a fireside chat at MEET Las Vegas in Las Vegas, Nev., on May 7, 2026. (Ian Maule/Getty Images)

Former Gov. Jim Hodges of South Carolina, the lead off state in the Democratic Party's 2028 presidential nominating calendar, told Politico, "I don’t see anything different myself. It seems like more of the same to me."

But Cardona, a veteran of the Bill Clinton administration, the Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama presidential campaigns who currently serves as a member of the Democratic National Committee, disagreed that Harris had failed to spell out what she would offer Democrats anxious for change.

"How can you state that she hasn’t done anything new or groundbreaking or talked about new initiatives or policies and then lay out exactly those policies — like proposing an expanded Supreme Court, lowering the voting age to 16, making D.C. and Puerto Rico states. Those are pretty groundbreaking policies!" Cardona told Fox News Digital, as she pointed to some of Harris' moves since the end of former President Joe Biden's administration.

Harris, the nation's first Black vice president, has also said that Black people should be "transactional voters," instead of automatically supporting Democratic candidates.

"She’s damned if she does and damned if she doesn’t," Cardona argued, adding that Harris "is still the most qualified person to be president of the United States that is mentioned as a possible candidate for 2028."

Harris has been crisscrossing the country this year, first on a book tour for her best-selling campaign memoir "107 Days" and currently to support fellow Democrats running in the midterm elections.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Former Vice President Kamala Harris joins Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a roundtable discussion at Birth Detroit on Sept. 22, 2026. (David Guralnick - Pool/Getty Images)

While Harris has teamed up with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and congressional nominees in her home state, some Democratic nominees running in red states made headlines in recent weeks by asking the former vice president not to campaign with them.

But Cardona said, "Harris has been out there nonstop talking to young voters, women voters, Black voters, Latino voters, and she has been asked by many candidates to come and campaign with them. She has focused her energies on winning the midterm elections. Can you imagine the backlash if she was out there focusing on herself and how she can remake the Democratic Party?"

Harris replaced Biden as the Democrats' 2024 presidential nominee after he ended his re-election bid following a disastrous debate performance against President Donald Trump. Her truncated three-month presidential campaign ended in defeat, with Trump narrowly sweeping all the key battleground states as he won back the White House.

If she runs a third time for president, Harris will enjoy instant name ID and plenty of goodwill from within her party. But she would also face a Democratic base trying to move past the 2024 election setbacks, and she would likely be part of a very crowded and competitive 2028 primary field.

But longtime Democratic strategist Michael Ceraso said that consultants "are not voters."

"I just don’t trust that the consulting class really has a finger on the electorate," he told Fox News Digital. "To listen to consultants saying Harris has blown it – presidential politics hasn’t really even started yet. These consultants are just getting soundbites."

"The third time was the charm and everybody said to Biden when he ran the third time, ‘why are you running.’ Well guess what, he ended up becoming the nominee and the president," he said. "Why can’t Harris look at that template and say ‘that can apply to me too.’"

By Georgia Loney

ABC South West WA

Topic:Invasive Species

Obelia Walker has mapped an enormous arum infestation through her work for Nature Conservation Margaret River. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Infestations of invasive arum lilies are worsening across WA's southern forests.

Private landowners say the WA government needs to step up eradication on public land.

The National Biosecurity Committee has included the arum on a list of 14 priority weeds, which could unlock new control methods.

The sea of white lilies carpeting the forest floor south of Margaret River is a picturesque view, but an ugly sight for conservationists.

The arum lily, considered one of the most damaging weeds in the country, was banned from sale in WA more than 20 years ago, but the rogue garden plant's infestation of forests across WA's South West shows no sign of slowing.

Arum lilies in Boranup Forest, south of Margaret River. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

More than 3,000 private landowners have requested help to eradicate the weed on their properties.

But there are questions over the WA government's willingness to do the same in the state's national parks.

In Boranup Forest, 300km south of Perth, Obelia Walker has mapped an enormous arum infestation through her work for Nature Conservation Margaret River.

Arum lilies are a major issue in sections of the Boranup forest. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

The organisation is co-ordinating a three-year blitz helping private landholders control the spread of lilies on their properties, funded by the WA government.

Those efforts have been successful, but she is worried about the infestation on public land.

Obelia Walker says arum lilies are causing problems in native forest, but key areas are being protected. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"If you think about where the majority of diversity happens in the forest, it's in the understorey," she said.

The arum lily is worsening in the Tuart Forest National Park, near Busselton, conservationists say. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Further north, in the Ludlow Tuart Forest near Busselton, local volunteer Des Donnelly has petitioned the Cook government to do more about the national park infestation.

"It's probably worse than it ever was," he said.

Mr Donnelly was behind a petition presented to state parliament earlier this year, calling for government agencies to do more to fight the flower in the forest

Arum lilies on the roadside in Tuart National Park near Busselton. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"It's a token effort if you like; Main Roads do a little bit, DBCA do what they can do with their small budget," he said.

Glen Taylor's beef farm sits opposite the Boranup National Park, where there is a large infestation.

Glen Taylor says arum lilies are infesting the forest neighbouring his property. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

He has managed to all but eradicate the lily from his own land, but it still encroaches at the borders.

"That is where it's a struggle," he said.

The state government's focus is on controlling arum lily in priority areas, rather than trying to eradicate the plant, prompting criticism from conservationists.

But a state government spokesperson said eradication was not realistic, with more than $2.6 million granted to arum lily control programs across the South West over the past nine years.

Arum lilies can be seen throughout the Ludlow Tuart National Park. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"While arum lily can be managed, it is not currently considered feasible to completely eradicate the species from the landscape due to its extensive distribution and ability to regenerate and spread," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said it had undertaken control across areas in the Tuart Forest National Park, Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park, Wooditjup National Park, Yelverton National Park, and selected state forest and nature reserve sites.

Conservationists agreed that the National Biosecurity Committee's inclusion of the arum lily on its list of Nationally Established Weed Priorities could lead to more innovative methods of control.

Nature Conservation's Obelia Walker hoped it would unlock funding for research into more cutting-edge methods to tackle the weed.

"It might be something quite novel; it might be a fungus or a disease, but it's an exciting space."

Arum lilies are infesting the Boranup forest. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Invasive Species Council policy director Carol Booth said the war on the lily was ultimately reliant on political will.

"I mean, the arum lily is one of the classic examples in Australia of a garden plant that's just gone rogue," she said.

"Which of these weeds are our state and federal governments prepared to put funding into to generate a much more collaborative and concerted approach to managing their risks?"

It has been said that a society should be judged not by how it treats its outstanding citizens but by how it treats people who break the law.

I research prisons and am interested in what incarceration reveals about the relationship between the state and the people in its care.

By this standard, the UK and Denmark tell very different stories. In 2025, Denmark’s prison population stood at around 69 people per 100,000 residents, compared with about 170 per 100,000 in the UK – roughly two and a half times higher.

One way to understand this difference is through welfare. With its wide range of universal welfare state services such as heavily subsidised daycare, free healthcare, free education and high standards of public services, Denmark’s criminal justice system has traditionally placed greater emphasis on rehabilitation and reintegration. Prisoners retain the right to vote, maintain closer contact with family and are generally encouraged to participate in ordinary social life where possible.

Health Gap / Sundhedskløften is a collaborative series from The Conversation UK and Denmark’s Videnskab.dk exploring what the two countries can learn from each other when it comes to health and wellbeing.

From cycling and alcohol to inequality, healthcare and everyday habits, the series looks beyond hospitals and medical treatment to explore how culture, politics and society shape the way people live – and how healthy they are.

The UK, while still a welfare state, is more uneven in its provision. And these  social differences are reflected in criminal justice policy. This results in higher incarceration rates in the UK, as well as more challenging prison conditions and a stronger emphasis on punishment and deterrence.

Indeed, my previous research, comparing prisons in England and Wales with another Nordic country, Norway, found that imprisonment in the UK is often experienced as unpredictable and austere. Norway’s system, meanwhile – which is closer to the Danish system – felt more structured and respectful.

Yet this difference in approach is only relatively recent. After the second world war, both countries used open prisons widely, spearheaded humane and progressive politics and had low imprisonment rates.

From the 1980s onwards, however, the UK increasingly moved towards a more punitive approach to criminal justice. Under Margaret Thatcher’s government and subsequent administrations, prison populations grew substantially while conditions in many prisons deteriorated.

The question is: which works best? Tough on crime policies that dramatically increase the prison population, or welfare-based decision making with an emphasis on rehabilitation?

On the surface, the outcomes can look surprisingly similar. Around 30% of prisoners released in Denmark go on to reoffend, compared with 29% in England and Wales. But that comparison changes when you look more closely.

For those serving short sentences of under a year, reoffending is around 34% in Denmark. Whereas this figure almost doubles for the UK, with roughly 66% of prisoners going on to reoffend.

The disruption caused by short-term imprisonment – loss of housing, employment, relationships and social stability – is particularly severe in the UK, where prisoners often leave custody with limited support.

Yet Denmark should not be romanticised. Danish prisons may be safer, more humane and more “survivable” than many prisons in the UK, but they also contain notable problems.

In Denmark, prisons have faced criticism over the use of pre-trial isolation, lack of care for women in custody, and the treatment of gang-affiliated prisoners.

In January 2026, the death of a prisoner in North Jutland triggered large protests from prisoners and their families – amid concerns that serious health issues were not properly addressed. The prisoner was reportedly experiencing intense abdominal and stomach pain in the days leading up to this death. With claims from inmates that he repeatedly sought medical attention before dying in his cell.

Denmark’s prison service has also lost around 30% of its staff over the past decade, with prisons running at or above capacity.

The UK system has faced similar problems in recent years. Around 3,000 prison officers leave their roles every year in England and Wales, contributing to a constant cycle of recruitment and turnover. Combined with overcrowding, lack of rehabilitative initiatives and rising violence, it leaves many prisons stretched thin.

These pressures are reshaping daily life inside. In Denmark, open prisons – once seen as central to the rehabilitative approach – are changing. Increasingly, low-risk prisoners serve their sentences in the community under electronic tag, meaning open prisons now tend to be filled with more vulnerable and complex cases.

Drugs can be an issue. Staff are also often young and still training, meaning that maintaining order can be a challenge.

In both countries, high-security prisoners can spend up to 22 hours a day in their cells due to staff shortages and restricted regimes. It’s a reminder that very different systems can produce similarly harsh conditions under pressure.

Bjørn*, a prisoner I spoke with during my fieldwork in a high-security prison in Denmark, was often transferred between prisons where he was kept in strict conditions because he was considered a “difficult” prisoner.

Reflecting on his previous sentence, he said: “I was angry with the authorities when I went in. When I got out, I hated them”. His experience illustrates how punishment that relies heavily on containment can create prisons that are more volatile for both staff and prisoners.

But as my research  also found, in Denmark, imprisonment is often seen in more conditional terms.

As, Noah* – another of of the prisoners I spoke with –  put it, it’s almost like a “contract” between the individual and the state, where efforts to change are meant to be met with a real chance of release. In other words, Danes have high expectations of their state, even when it punishes them.

That reflects the wider level of trust in public institutions found in Denmark: around 60% of Danes say they trust their government, compared with about 33% in the UK.

In England and Wales, prisoners and staff alike describe a system shaped by overcrowding, staff shortages and instability, with fewer opportunities for rehabilitation.

In this sense, the comparison between Denmark and the UK is not a straightforward story of “humane” versus “punitive” systems. But something more complicated about trust, expectations and pressure.

That said, the Danish Government has recently launched a new strategy for punishment with longer sentences alongside more rehabilitative initiatives. These proposals have been met with concern as to whether a more rehabilitative model can survive when resources are stretched.

In the end, though, the differences between Denmark and the UK are not fixed. Because prison systems are not just shaped by national philosophies on punishment, but also by the political choices that determine whether rehabilitation is adequately funded and supported.

*Prisoners’ names have been changed

A historic Black church in South Los Angeles that had been severely damaged in two previous fires went up in flames for a third time before sunrise Monday.

A fire at the vacant house of worship at East 27th and Paloma streets was reported just after 3:30 a.m., and the two-story wooden building “looks like it’s going to be a complete tear-down,” said Jennifer Middleton, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department.

Flames ripped through the roof, and it took about 180 firefighters more than an hour and 36 minutes to knock down the blaze at 1001 E. 27th St.

An arson investigation is underway, Middleton said.

“Luckily, there are no injuries,” she said, adding that heavy equipment crews were on scene early Monday doing some demolition work. The building, she said, has been red-tagged. While there potentially is smoke or water damage to some neighboring structures, the fire was contained to the church.

The former Crouch Memorial Church of God in Christ was built in 1905, according to property records, and is part of a historic Black neighborhood, the 27th Street Historic District, that is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

It first burned in October 2013 in a massive blaze during which two Los Angeles firefighters were injured.

When firefighters arrived that morning, they saw flames shooting from the attic. Within 15 minutes of their arrival, portions of the attic and second floor collapsed, trapping a firefighter in heavily burning debris and forcing him to use his emergency air canister to breathe, according to an LAFD significant incident summary report.

“I got fire all around me ... I got fire all around me,” he could be heard saying over emergency radio transmissions before his colleagues carried him to safety. Another firefighter involved in the rescue was briefly evaluated for injuries, the report said.

A third firefighter was injured by what he said felt like an electric shock while he was on an aerial ladder spraying water onto the building.

Fire officials said that blaze appeared to have been accidental. At the time, Lawrence Magee, then 66, who has been the church’s pastor since 2011, said he may have unintentionally started the fire after he turned on a gas heater, telling reporters outside the charred building: “I feel terrible.”

“The historic church suffered grave damage and is considered a total loss monetarily,” the 2013 LAFD report read.

But the blighted, white-painted structure stood for more than a decade. Graffiti covered its charred facade, and it became a source of frustration for the neighborhood, attracting squatters and illegal garbage dumping.

The dilapidated building burned in another fire in 2024.

The abandoned Romanesque Revival-style building has been the source of numerous complaints to the city’s Department of Building and Safety since the initial fire. Last month, the department ordered the building’s owner to “immediately remove all fired damaged debris that pose a Present, immenent, extreme and immediate hazard or danger to life or limb, health or safety.”

Property records show Crouch Memorial Church of God in Christ as the property’s most recent owner. Magee could not be reached for comment.
