Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef imports

Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.

In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.

Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.

With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.

On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.

Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.

The cattle market tanked immediately.

"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."

"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.

Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.

That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.

Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.

Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.

Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs

The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.

And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.

Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.

"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.

Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.

Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.

Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market

The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.

But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.

"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.

Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.

"It really makes a guy think," he said.

A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.

But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.

"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.

Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.

"The daily upchargeâ¦ is kind of painful," he said.

"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."

Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.

But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.

He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.

"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball

Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.

But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.

That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.

Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.

He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.

That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.

"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.

An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".

Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".

Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry

But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.

"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."

But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".

What are the US midterms? A simple guide

The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope

Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".

But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed.

"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."

Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"

Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.

"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.

Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."

Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.

Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.

But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.

Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter

"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.

He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.

"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbersâ¦ I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"

Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.

"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."

Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state

All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.

On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.

Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - do not pause for politics.

Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.

"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

After months of questions from The Intercept, the U.S. military finally acknowledged the March death of Maj. Sorffly Davius.

The Pentagon quietly acknowledged additional Iran war deaths on Friday evening after The Intercept repeatedly demanded an explanation for inaccurate statistics on a War Department website tracking U.S. casualties from the conflict.

Almost 900 U.S. troops have been wounded or killed in the war with Iran, according to the official Pentagon count, including the two deaths added on Friday. This raises the Pentagon’s total to 21 dead.

The additional war dead include Maj. Sorffly Davius, a signals and communication officer with the New York Army National Guard who was assigned to the headquarters of the 42nd Infantry Division and died while on duty in Camp Buehring, Kuwait, on March 6. For more than six months, The Intercept has raised Davius’s case in dozens of emails and phone conversations with Pentagon officials and publicly in 10 articles.

The Pentagon recently revamped the website of the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS — which provides official counts of dead and wounded for Congress and the White House — to include more detailed casualty category tables. But it initially listed no “non-hostile” illness or injury fatalities, despite the Pentagon announcing in March that Davius died “as a result of a non-combat related incident.”

At first, the military claimed that Davius was involved in another operation instead of Epic Fury — the original designation of the Iran war. As the state’s public servant pension shortfall soars to at least $153 billion, the California Post can reveal that more than 63,000 retired public servants are being paid at least $100,000 a year from the California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS), the largest public pension fund in the US.

The massive gravy train — and recent efforts to further increase pension payouts — has been slammed by local elected officials who also benefit from CalPERS for straining local government budgets when they’re forced to pick up the tab for rising pensions.

“In the 1990s and the early 2000s, similar pension packages nearly bankrupted this state and many of our local municipalities,” Santa Barbara County Supervisor Bob Nelson told lawmakers last year, noting his county has had to pay out an extra $100 million annually to keep up with rising pensions.

“Those payments came at real costs: Reductions to pay public safety staffing and fewer resources to address mental health, homelessness and criminal justice reform,” he added.

The 63,107 pensioners earning six figures are more than double the amount from 2018, when more than 26,000 were in the $100K-plus club. Two decades ago, in 2005, just 1,841 retirees were pocketing six-figure pensions, the Orange County Register reported.

The pension bonanza has been labeled a financial ticking time bomb by experts who spoke with the California Post, after to a decision by former Democrat Gov. Gray Davis in 1999 to sign a law significantly increasing public pension benefits for state employees.

“If I knew then what I know now, I would never have signed SB 400,” Davis said in 2012, referring to the law.

Much of CalPERS is a defined benefit pension system funded by a mix of employee contributions, investment growth and contributions by government employers — in other words, taxpayer dollars.

“The system is $153 billion short on assets needed to pay for promised benefits, the largest single pension debt in the country,” Zachary Christensen, who leads the Pension Integrity Project at the Reason Foundation, told The Post.

“The growing number of retirees receiving lavish public pension benefits in California rightfully frustrates taxpayers and will likely worsen in the years ahead,” Christensen added.

The average annual pension benefit is $44,209, according to a Post analysis. But the number of top-tier earners — those raking in at least $300,000 in benefits — has grown in recent years.

In 2023, there were just 21. Last year, the number grew to 36.

Topping the list is Curtis Ishii, who was a managing investment director for fixed income at CalPERS itself. He collected $462,784 last year and has been one of the biggest recipients since he retired in 2018 after more than 40 years in public service.

One reason for his big benefits: His last paycheck in 2017 was $688,000. Government pensions are calculated with a formula based on annual salary and years of service. Investment officers are among the highest-paid California state employees.

Michael D. Johnson, a former Solano County administrator, was not far behind with his $426,028 pension last year. Johnson became Solano County administrator in 1992 at age 43 with 19 years of experience in the public sector. His total gross pay in 2010, the last full year he worked for the county, was $354,197.

His annual payment has grown over the years, as CalPERS applies annual cost-of-living increases. Johnson was previously the highest earner when he had a $372,000 pension in 2019.

The last of the big three is Steve Maguin, who had a 23-year career in solid waste management and was chief engineer plus general manager of Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts. In 2012, he held a salary of $125,693. He received $418,614 last year from CalPERS.

Maguin passed away in January, according to a LinkedIn post, after retiring in 2012.

“I talked with him not long after his retirement and he seemed happy and fulfilled,” one user commented on the news of his death.

The rest of the CalPERS beneficiaries who got lavish payments totaling more than $350,000 last year are:

Not all recipients have fully retired, with some moving on to non-government jobs. For example, Di Stasio is listed as the president of the Large Public Power Council, where he advocates for public power systems in Washington, DC.

Huge annual pensions may eventually phase out after California lawmakers passed a 2013 law that ties public pensions to IRS limits.

Still, there are many going into retirement with pensions formed before the 2013 rules went into effect. CalPERS’ total payout has increased in recent years, from $29.1 billion in 2021-22 to $34.6 billion in 2024-25. The total number of members receiving pensions also grew.

All that will put strain on CalPERS to keep up with its benefits obligations, despite a banner year in investment returns.

“That has been the question that has been discussed for years and years in all public sector jobs,” said Dr. Jeffrey Goodrich, a professor with UCLA’s Financial Management Program and a wealth advisor at JCG Private Wealth Management. “They’re supported by the communities or the state, or the cities, or the municipalities, and those numbers are getting bigger and bigger all the time, and they’ve reached tremendous sums.”

Goodrich said the rising number of bulging pensions could be attributed to more people taking advantage of the benefits and staying longer in public service. People may also just be getting higher salaries, which the pension formula is based on, he added.

Christensen blamed former Gov. Davis, who along with state lawmakers in 1999 gave all public workers and retirees a massive pension benefit increase.

“The impact of this decision has played out over decades; workers who were just getting started in their careers at the time are now reaching retirement and cashing in on their sweetened CalPERS benefits,” Christensen said.

Back then, Davis approved a massive expansion of benefits as the pension system was flush with cash. CalPERS had assured then there would be no cost due to “booming stock market and investment strategies.”

The changes enabled state and local government employees to stop working at an earlier age to collect more retirement pay and made more lucrative pension calculations retroactive.

But economic crises occurred, from the dot-com bubble to the Great Recession. The increased benefits combined with investment losses caused annual government contributions to CalPERS to jump from $1.6 billion in 1999 to $26.7 billion this fiscal year.

Despite the ballooning cost, unions were still pushing for pension increases as recently as this year. Gov. Gavin Newsom ended up vetoing a bill last month that would have expanded pension benefits for police officers and firefighters.

“This is an era of California history I do not wish to repeat,” Newsom wrote in his veto statement, citing the pension crisis before the 2013 law.

Large public pension payouts may continue for at least another decade before the group of workers most affected by the state’s 2013 pension reforms starts retiring, Christensen explained. Until then, unions — a major political force in Sacramento — will continue seeking higher payouts.

“Very strong unions make sure their members get the compensation they deserve, and you’re hoping that the city, or the municipalities, or the counties have good negotiators on their side,” UCLA’s Goodrich said.

“That’s an unknown factor to say, can we do this forever, and the answer is I don’t know,” he added.

Gold Coast Suns have consolidated their spot in the top-four with a 22-point win over flag contenders Melbourne in Mackay.

Geelong beat GWS by 63 points to go top of the ladder, while Adelaide downed Richmond by 32 points in Melbourne.

North Melbourne can re-take top spot if they beat Fremantle on Sunday.

Gold Coast have rubber-stamped their AFLW top-four credentials with a historic 22-point victory over Melbourne.

The Suns posted their sixth straight win on Saturday night, faring better in sweltering heat at Mackay's Great Barrier Reef Arena to down the Demons 9.7 (61) to 5.9 (39).

Gold Coast had not beaten Melbourne in their four previous clashes since the Suns entered the women's competition in 2020.

"It's been a long few years for us and we've been slowly building every year," Suns co-captain Lucy Single told Fox Footy after the landmark triumph.

"So to kind of get that win under our belt has been so awesome and I think that's really boosted our confidence."

The Suns find themselves sitting pretty with three rounds left before finals, drawing level with Melbourne at 7-2.

Melbourne took a three-point lead into quarter-time, but Gold Coast kicked away in the second term and did not look back.

Midfielder Charlie Rowbottom had a game-high 33 possessions and six clearances as Ava Usher, Mikayla Nurse and Havana Harris (two goals apiece) all fired up forward.

Despite the mercury hovering in the mid-20s, Usher said the Suns were not fazed by the conditions.

"We knew it was going to be a really tough arm-wrestle and in the end we just got over the line in really hot conditions," the first-year Sun said.

"We're pretty used to it."

Adelaide had too much firepower for Richmond in the earlier game, winning 9.8 (62) to 4.6 (30) at Melbourne's Princes Park.

The 32-point victory put the Crows back in the finals hunt at 4-5, although they remain just outside the eight with three games of round nine to play.

Prolific ball-winner Ebony Marinoff collected 40 disposals, 13 tackles and a goal.

It's been an AFLW season to forget for St Kilda, but Saturday's win over Collingwood has given departing Saints coach Nick Dal Santo a perfect send-off.

The 40-possession game was one shy of her career-best mark.

The Crows captain said it had been a tough week following a 14-point Showdown loss to Port Adelaide.

"I'd be lying [to say] we didn't know what was on the line tonight," Marinoff said.

"But really proud of the girls' efforts just to really start well … because we hadn't over the last fortnight."

Earlier in the day, Geelong took top spot — at least for now — with a 63-point win over GWS at Kardinia Park, with Jacqueline Parry and Aishling Moloney each kicking four goals.

The Cats will fall back to second, however, if North Melbourne beats Fremantle on Sunday.

The other early game saw St Kilda win their first game for the season, with a two-point win over Collingwood at Moorabbin.

The illegal migrant shot by ICE agents in a chaotic Bronx showdown terrorized his former neighbors with a machete—and terrified residents said Saturday they are universally relieved the violent gangbanger has finally been taken off the streets.

Oscar Belgal, 28, who federal authorities said is a “criminal illegal alien” from the Dominican Republic with alleged ties to the violent Trinitarios street gang, wreaked havoc in the halls of the Washington Heights apartment building where he lived until about a year ago, according to locals.

“He’s a menace to society,” one shaken resident said of Belgal — who Mayor Zohran Mamdani outrageously called a “New Yorker,” whose release he tried to negotiate as he railed against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“I spoke to him once and told him, ‘Look, you need to be more submissive because I see you acting too reckless’ … He thought he was a tough guy,” the resident told The Post.

The former neighbor, a man from the Dominican Republic who withheld his name, recalled one of Belgal’s most unhinged outbursts while living there — in which he pulled a machete on another resident’s nephew.

He claimed Belgal got into a fight with the man outside the building last year, prompting him to whip out the deadly weapon.

The neighbor also claimed Belgal, who he described as arrogant and smug, previously dodged ICE by running down one of the building’s two fire escapes.

“They were looking for him. It seems he had a pending case; Immigration goes after people who have committed crimes,” he said. “Immigration is just doing its job. They go after those who have committed crimes.”

Belgal’s rap sheet includes a 2023 armed robbery conviction and a 2025 arrest for allegedly selling lethal drugs like fentanyl, cocaine and heroin in a case that remains open. His most recent run-in with the law was Thursday when two plainclothes ICE agents, with guns drawn, approached the front left side of the gray Honda CR-V he was driving as he peeled out of a parking spot on 225th Street in The Bronx.

One punched and smashed the glass of the driver’s side window. Marcos Charles, the head of ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division, said Belgal “accelerated” at the agents, “smashing” into two of them, which was not captured on the CCTV footage obtained by The Post Friday.

Agents caught up with Belgal about half a block away on Marble Hill Ave outside the C&G Gourmet Deli before bullets rang and he was shot in the neck, according to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch.

His 5-year-old son, who was in the backseat of the vehicle, was unharmed. Belgal is expected to recover.

On Saturday, protests erupted in Midtown in support of the alleged gangbanger, with anti-ICE rioters holding signs demanding “justice for Oscar Belgal” and to “abolish ICE.” Other posters called for Tisch to be fired.

“He’s putting his son at risk. He’s got legal trouble, yet he drives around with his son in the car?” Belgal’s outraged former neighbor asked. “No, I don’t think that’s right. If he owes a debt to society, he should pay it…He was a danger to society.”

After being taken into custody, Belgal was transported to New York-Presbyterian Allen Hospital in stable condition. He was discharged at 9:58 p.m. and taken by ICE to Delaney Hall in Newark, NJ at 10:43 p.m.  He was transported to Metropolitan Detention Center (MDC) in Brooklyn on Friday.

“Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible extensive impacts across San Diego County,” the weather service warned.

Anastasia Tsioulcas

The blocked-off entrance to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Oct. 1. The center has been shut to the public since September.
                
                    
                    Saul Loeb/AFP/via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

The Kennedy Center has named Rick Canny, a talent manager who has worked with acts including ZZ Top and former Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. His appointment came despite complaints from staff about his business practices as a consultant for the arts institution.

According to an email obtained by NPR sent to high-level staff Thursday, Matt Floca, the center's executive director and chief operating officer, announced that Canny would be the center's new artistic director. Canny has served as a consultant to the Kennedy Center since shortly after President Trump became the institution's chairman in February 2025.

Floca has no background in arts administration, programming or fundraising, in contrast to chief administrators at similar performing arts venues around the country. He was previously head of facilities at the Kennedy Center before being promoted in March, and holds a degree in construction management.

Floca wrote: "Rick will advise me and the broader leadership team on artistic strategy, business practices, presenting and talent curation, ticketing and pricing models, media opportunities, and programming sponsorships."

Floca also wrote: "Since April 2025, Rick has worked with the Center as a consultant through his firm, Favor the Artist, including serving as creative lead for the Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize. He will continue in this capacity while serving as the Center's Artistic Director."

The Kennedy Center is mostly closed, but it says it will maintain a small amount of public and educational programming, while the entire closure is being contested in federal court. The previous head of programming came and left within two weeks in January.

Arts administrators around the country have told NPR that booking performances for performing arts centers is done years in advance.

The Kennedy Center did not respond to NPR's requests for comment on Canny's appointment, but confirmed the contents of the email. Canny also did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Favor the Artist's website does not include any information about its client roster or about the firm's history. The published lists of his professional background indicate that Canny has little experience in programming the kinds of performers more typically booked at a venue such as the Kennedy Center, including marquee contemporary solo performers and groups, orchestras, and dance and theater troupes.

NPR has obtained an internal memo written in March by the center's then-senior director of music programming, Sammy Miller, raising concerns about fees and expenses charged by Canny. NPR has reached out to Miller for comment, but did not receive a reply.

In that memo, sent to Floca and the Kennedy Center's human resources department, Miller said that during one month in early 2026, Canny had charged the center $30,000 in consulting fees. And in another month, Canny had charged over $28,000 in fees and travel expenses, including two first-class round-trip flights between Los Angeles and Washington, D.C.

The Kennedy Center did not reply to NPR's request for comment regarding staff concerns about Canny. In a statement to The New York Times on Friday, the center said that the $30,000 fee "did not reflect Mr. Canny's current agreement," but did not provide specifics. The institution also told the Times that Canny's travel expenses had been reviewed.

Miller wrote that he had previously tried to resolve his concerns through the center's general counsel and its finance office, but "both offices appear to be protecting Mr. Canny."

In its recent public statements and court filings, the Kennedy Center has repeatedly claimed to be on the verge of bankruptcy. Last month, Trump said that the arts institution has lost "hundreds of millions" of dollars. Trump has not offered evidence to support that claim.

The Kennedy Center remains shut to the public while Trump and the center's board, most of whom were hand-selected by the president, fight in a federal court to shutter the institution for two years for a large-scale renovation. Last month, Trump threatened to tear down the center if his name is not prominently displayed on the building.

The end of Roe v. Wade in 2022 was supposed to be devastating for abortion access across the US. Thousands of women every month—the ones who could afford it—would be forced to travel long distances to receive care. Many more women would be forced to continue pregnancies they didn’t want and couldn’t afford. The crisis would be worst in the South, the thinking went, because right-wing lawmakers were competing to see who could pass the most draconian bans.

Then something astonishing happened: In the four years since Roe’s demise, the number of abortions rose by almost 20 percent.

It’s one of the paradoxes of the Dobbs era: While abortion rights have been drastically curtailed in much of the country, abortion access has exploded. Galvanized by the extremism of the Supreme Court’s decision, reproductive health advocates have built an entire healthcare, legal, and financing infrastructure that has made abortions possible for hundreds of thousands of women in some of the most conservative parts of the US.

In this package, we look at the surprising resilience of the abortion access movement—and at how abortion opponents, including Students for Life’s Kristan Hawkins, are doubling down on their hardline agenda. At the center of the post-Dobbs story is the growing availability of abortion pills, which now account for almost two-thirds of all abortions in the US. “Medication abortion is here to stay,” one leading telehealth provider says. “You can’t put this genie back in a bottle.”

St Kilda gave departing AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo the perfect send-off with a drought-breaking two-point home win over Collingwood.

The victory was St Kilda's first of the AFLW season. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Ashley Centra, who gathered 25 touches for the Pies, kicked a goal in the final 30 seconds to cut the gap to two points, but the Saints held on.

A wild video captured a suburban New York highway boss being restrained as he screamed at a town supervisor during a press conference Thursday — sparking a police report and a probe into workplace violence.

Clarkstown Highway Superintendent Bob Milone is seen exploding on Town Supervisor George Hoehmann during a public announcement over repairs on a trailway around Congers Lake, in the clip filmed by the Rockland Daily.

“What you say to me, what you say to me? … Who the hell do you think you’re talking to, George? You could bully everybody else in this town,” Milone yelled at Hoehmann as a man tried to restrain him from attacking the town supervisor.

“You could bully everybody else in this town. Stop bullying people, George!” he yelled before finally walking away from the scene.

The town of Clarkstown — a suburban enclave in Rockland County — confirmed Friday that a police report was filed and a formal workplace investigation has been launched over the “widely circulated” video of the spat.

It is unclear who filed the police report.

“Following the incident, a police report was filed, and the town’s Safety Compliance Officer was notified. A formal workplace violence investigation has been launched as a result of this video,” the town said in a statement.

“The Town of Clarkstown takes violations of workplace safety and threats or acts of violence seriously, and will thoroughly review the matter.”

The statement added that the town provides annual workplace violence safety training.

California High Speed Rail bigwigs reportedly billed taxpayers for unexplained late-night trips to and from CEO Ian Choudri’s Folsom home, along with rides to local bars and restaurants — as reps face tough questions about nearly $600,000 in blown expenses revealed in a recent audit.

Two rail consultants, Denver-based Nossaman LLP attorney Brent Butzin and KPMG director Thierry Prate, were reimbursed for Lyft rides at odd hours last September, even after 1 a.m in the morning in one instance, according to receipts obtained by CBS Sacramento.

The two highly-paid consultants were responsible for a dozen rideshare trips to or from a quiet residential road where Choudri, who nets $638,943 in annual comp to run the troubled bullet train project, owns a home.

Another dozen rides were linked to bars or restaurants in Folsom near a pricey surf ‘n turf joint, Land Ocean Steak House, that Choudri is known to frequent, per CBS.

The receipts were part of a bombshell Inspector General audit that found $592,900 in “unallowable” expenses incurred by consultants, including rideshare trips to Tiki bars and an “escape room” and first-class flight upgrades.

The revelations added fresh scrutiny to the multibillion-dollar bullet train project that’s been bogged down by lengthy delays and massive cost overruns, with one estimate pegging the total cost at $231 billion.

An updated business plan from the rail authority estimated the cost at $126.3 billion.

The late-night rides identified by CBS were vaguely explained as “related to work with Ian,” according to a email from KPMG.

In one case, a back-and-forth ensued between Butzin and a rail authority staffer who questioned the expenses, with the lawyer reportedly arguing that Choudri requested his presence.

The rail authority did, however, reject one $94.39 pizza delivery order that was sent for reimbursement.

Choudri, along with other staffers, appeared at a Friday meeting of the rail agency’s Board of Directors to discuss the findings in the inspector general’s audit, which examined $2 million in travel expenses from four major contractors: Law firm Nossaman LLP, KPMG, AECOM-Flour Joint Venture and SYSTRA/TYPSA Joint Venture.

Members of the board — including recently appointed Gavin Newsom allies Steve Kawa and Jason Elliott — voiced exasperation with the blown expenses.

“You can’t fly first class when you’re on state travel, you don’t take an Uber black SUV,” said Elliott, a former Newsom deputy chief of staff.

A statement from the High Speed Rail Authority didn’t directly address the unexplained trips, but claimed the agency is updating its internal cost controls.

Staffers at the Friday meeting vowed to recover the misspent taxpayer money. “As an agency entrusted with stewarding public resources, the Authority is reinforcing its travel approval and reimbursement processes to ensure every consultant trip is appropriate, justified and fully compliant with state policy,” rail spokesperson Daniela Contreras said in an email. “Only travel that is pre‑approved, within contract scope and consistent with state regulations will be eligible for reimbursement,” Contreras said.

An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police.

The AI reportedly submitted this incorrect information to a public Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tip line on July 18, but Anthropic didn’t discover the behavior until September 28. The police had not seen the tip because it was marked as spam.

Anthropic notified the PPD about the incident on Wednesday and met with the department the following day.

“The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the PPD said in a statement to 6abc.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the PPD elaborated on the incident in an emailed press release shared with TechCrunch.

“According to Anthropic, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted false information concerning an unsolved homicide. The submission, dated July 18, 2026, at 11:27 p.m., purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said.

As autonomous AI agents are increasingly made available to consumers, this incident highlights the danger of giving AI the ability to carry out tasks without any human supervision.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been especially vocal about his belief that AI development should be slowed down so that labs can implement adequate guardrails. Perhaps this stance was informed, in part, by witnessing his company’s tools submit false homicide tips.

These issues are not exclusive to Anthropic. OpenAI recently revealed that one of its models acted unexpectedly during a test and hacked the AI dataset platform Hugging Face, exposing critical vulnerabilities in its software. As AI models continue to be granted unchecked access to people’s computers and login credentials, this problem is expected to persist.

“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the PPD added. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.”

The PPD said that Anthropic plans to publish a report with more information about the incident and other instances of unintended model behavior on Friday.

Art & Design

October 09, 2026

I recently came across an article published by the Data Visualisation Society's Nightingale magazine that captures a niche but wonderful corner of a largely bygone era of stamps, graphic design, and data visualisation as political communications.

Its author, Julie Peasley, assembled 180 stamps from around the world featuring charts and other data visuals from 88 countries. Among them are examples from across the Middle East and North Africa. Together, they offer a shed light into how the region's governments chose to illustrate growth through future projections and economic indicators.

I reviewed a set containing 38 entries from 14 countries from 1940 to 2015. Looking into the stamps, I uncovered a rich snapshot of the time the stamp was issued and the context behind the beautiful graphics, colours and charts.

Here are a few of the most striking and informative stamps.

Census stamps were a common feature in the database. At the turn of the last century, many Middle Eastern countries' populations were exploding, and the administrative task of keeping track was a huge national undertaking. Many countries chose to mark these occasions with special commemorative stamps.

Iraq's 1987 census stamp is a busy composition highlighting the diversity of the country, with illustrations representing rural and urban workers. Behind them, a line graph presents a population count through the visual language of a modern government.

But it's important to remember another context. According to Human Rights Watch, “the machinery of genocide was set in motion” against Iraqi Kurds in March 1987, and that year’s census became part of it ahead of the Anfal campaign. In that context, the stamp is a reminder that counting a population can also be a means of documenting who is wanted – and who isn't.

Egypt’s 1976 population and housing census stamp brings people and their surroundings into the same frame. Combining the height of the construction boom showing a city scape in a turquoise backdrop, figures gather along the bottom and lines traverse a grid marked with years and numbers.

It was issued during president Anwar Sadat’s infitah, or “open-door” policy, introduced in 1974 to attract Arab and foreign investment. Egypt was changing its economic direction and the stamp’s buildings and statistical grid can be read as a small picture of that ambition to modernise.

Kuwait’s census stamp shows a family of four in traditional dress, beside a pink outline of the country and beneath a rising line chart, combining both a family portrait and statistics.

Issued in 1965, only four years after independence in 1961, it captures a country changing quickly.

Kuwait’s population had more than doubled since 1957, reaching about 467,000 by 1965, with non-Kuwaitis making up slightly more than half of its residents. Behind the simple family illustration was a much bigger story of oil, migration and the building of a modern state.

The UAE’s 1980 population census stamp is beautiful in its illustrative simplicity. A family stands against a pink grid, in traditional dress.

The UAE was still less than a decade old at the time and this count followed its first general census in 1975. In Abu Dhabi alone, the population more than doubled between those two counts, from about 212,000 to 452,000.

Qatar marked the Mena Economic Conference of 1997 with a stamp featuring an artistic line chart, turning the visual language of economic growth into a commemorative and memorable design.

Held in Doha in November 1997, the conference belonged to a series launched in the wake of the Oslo Accords, with hopes that closer economic ties would support regional peace. The stamp’s optimism sits against a much more complicated political moment.

Marking 100 years of the Egyptian stock exchange, the design combines a rising graph with a sweeping curved arrow. This shows a colourful composition of movement, fluctuation and forward momentum. The anniversary reaches back to the exchange’s establishment in 1903.

This UAE stamp, with “Growth Monitoring” written in Arabic and English, was issued as part of Unicef’s Child Survival Campaign, reflecting a major public-health push of the 1980s.

Unicef promoted simple, affordable measures – regular growth monitoring, breastfeeding, immunisation and oral rehydration therapy – to help more children survive their early years.

It is a strong example of data visualisation serving a practical purpose. Growth charts are still used today to track children’s development and spot when they might need help.

Sudan’s World Statistics Day stamp takes a broader view of what data can do. Colourful triangles and circles accompany the phrase “Better Data, Better Lives”, putting the emphasis on how statistics can improve people’s lives.

The timing matters. In 2015, the UN adopted the Sustainable Development Goals, setting targets on poverty, health, education and much more. Reliable statistics were essential to knowing where countries stood and whether they were making progress. Sudan’s stamp carries the theme of that year’s World Statistics Day into a small, colourful design.

By

Reshma Kirpalani

Arístides Fernandez-Garcia (left) and Yasmany Moreno-De Armas were deported to the Central African Republic on July 30, 2026.
                
                    
                    Yasmany Moreno-De Armas
                    
                
                hide caption

MIAMI — José Díaz, 85, had never asked his grand-nephew for a single thing.

But late last year, he noticed the baseball cap Arístides Fernandez-Garcia was wearing on his visit to New Jersey. He liked it.

Fernandez-Garcia promised himself that he'd give his great-uncle the cap after returning from a Miami hearing in his pending asylum case.

He never got the chance.

On Jan. 6 Fernandez-Garcia, a Cuban immigrant, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in a targeted operation at the courthouse in Miami.

He told NPR that as he moved through a maze of detention centers across the U.S., losing 60 pounds and witnessing shocking violence, he held hard onto his promise. When his great-uncle got sick, Fernandez-Garcia called him from detention.

"I would tell him: 'Stay strong, because I have to give you the hat,'" Fernandez-Garcia recalled. The old man would laugh.

Eight months later, Fernandez-Garcia sits in the living room of an apartment in the Central African Republic. He feels torn: guilty for giving Díaz hope, but resolved, nevertheless, to keep his promise.

"That is something I have to do in life before anything else happens to him," he says about his great-uncle. "I have to give him that hat."

Credit:  Reshma Kirpalani for NPR

Fernandez-Garcia is among the more than 25,000 people the Trump administration says it has deported to countries to which they have no ties. On Sept. 18, a federal appeals court ruled this "third country deportation" policy violates due process. The court said migrants weren't given enough notice or a meaningful chance to say they were afraid to be sent to another country. On Sept. 24, the Trump administration appealed that ruling to the Supreme Court.

In a statement to NPR, the Department of Homeland Security said "Third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets."

But NPR found no record of criminal charges in Florida against either Fernandez-Garcia or his roommate, Yasmany Noel Moreno-De Armas, who is also a Cuban immigrant deported by the U.S. Fernandez-Garcia didn't have a deportation order either. Both men say they don't feel safe returning to Cuba.

"I face punishment from the Cuban regime for having been a balsero — someone who fled Cuba by raft — and for trying to avail myself of the 'wet foot, dry foot' policy and enter the United States under that protection," said Moreno-De Armas.

DHS says people being deported to third countries receive "notice and assurances prior to their removal." DHS added that ICE obtains diplomatic assurances from destination countries that once people are deported they will be safe after they arrive.

But both men said they didn't know where they were going when they boarded the plane in Texas. From his shared apartment in the Central African Republic, Fernandez-Garcia showed NPR how he sat on the plane for 12 hours, his hands shackled together and chained to a belt around his waist. It wasn't until they landed and he looked out the window, he says, that he saw a flag. It was striped green, yellow and red, with a green star in the center. That's the flag of Senegal, he realized. They were in Africa.

"My mind just went blank," said Fernandez-Garcia. "I went blank because I realized that my life was out of my hands, like I didn't have control over my own life anymore. I still don't."

The men say they don't feel safe in the Central African Republic, a country the State Department warns Americans not to visit, citing risks of kidnapping, landmines and terrorism. The International Organization for Migration, a group affiliated with the United Nations, is providing protection for the deportees. Armed guards accompany them whenever they leave the complex. The IOM is also providing housing in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic. The deportees live four to an apartment. Fernandez-Garcia and Moreno-De Armas share a bedroom.

Their building neighbors a small market: low-slung buildings with concrete walls and corrugated-metal roofs. The road is unpaved and often muddy. They shop there twice a week for canned goods and water. When the power is on, the men talk to their families on WhatsApp, do interviews with reporters and make social media videos, trying to get their story out. Maybe that will help them return to the U.S., they think. Sometimes, viewers donate money. It helps them buy supplies for their shared apartment and minutes on their phones.

But two months after arriving, both men remain in limbo, unsure of their legal status or what comes next.

"We don't have documents that would allow us to work. They haven't given us a visa," said Moreno-De Armas. "We were deported from the United States to a third country and we're still detained."

Both men have gotten sick in Bangui. Fernandez-Garcia with malaria, which kept him weak in bed for days. Moreno-De Armas with high blood pressure, shortness of breath, and panic attacks when he heard his mother was in the hospital.

But what affects them most isn't the physical toll. It's time.

"Time with family, time with those people who have less time left, no, no, that can never be recovered again," said Fernandez-Garcia. "Not even with millions of dollars can that be recovered or bought."

The men know other "third country deportees" who have been in Africa for a long time. Like Roberto Mosquera, who has been imprisoned in Eswatini for over a year.

"This is all I do. Walk outside. Come back in. Fix some food. Lay down. Think," said Mosquera from his prison cell in Matsapha Correctional Complex, a high security prison. "You think about your kids, that life that you had before, the life that they took from you."

Mosquera has a criminal record and has already served his time in the U.S. But according to his lawyer, Alma David, he has no criminal charges in Eswatini. Mosquera also doesn't know if and when he'll be released. Since he's been imprisoned, his oldest sister died in America. So did his best friend. He's also going to miss his daughter's wedding.

"My youngest one's going to be the flower girl," said Mosquera. He looks away from the screen and sighs. "It's rough. I didn't expect this to happen at my age."

When de Moreno-De Armas' father got a call from his son that he had been deported to Africa, he felt like "the world fell on top of me," he says. Hiovany Moreno Noa sits in the backyard of his home in South Florida. Thick worry lines stretch across his forehead.

"If at least he were in a Spanish-speaking country, with more or less the same customs as us, then we could be a little more at ease," he says. "But there, we don't know anything. The little we do know is that it's a country that has been at war. It's a very dangerous country."

Credit:  Reshma Kirpalani for NPR

Moreno Noa tries to talk to his son every day. He sends what money he can though Western Union. He prays for him. But the separation is hard.

After Moreno-De Armas fled Cuba on a raft, years passed before he saw his family. They reunited in 2022.

"We went six years without seeing each other. Then we came to this country, and now we're being separated again," he said. "Every parent longs to have their children beside them. And that's why we suffer."

On Sept. 29, the Supreme Court put the appeal court's ruling on hold, clearing the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the legal battle plays out.

In Eswatini, Mosquera still dreams about the day he can leave Africa and return to his family. In the Central African Republic, Moreno-De Armas hasn't given up hope either, despite a recent curfew that kept him and his roommates indoors for three days.

"We're waiting for God to give us the opportunity to return to the United States," he says.

Fernandez-Garcia is not so sure. Hope exists, he says. But it disappears very easily.

He still loves America.

"I felt what freedom was like for the first time in my life. I felt what it was to dream for the first time in my life, to leave the Cuban bubble of the dictatorship," Fernandez-Garcia said about the U.S. "You can't judge a country by one particular moment."

But then he thinks about his great-uncle in New Jersey, who lives with his great-aunt. Like grandparents, they had taken care of him in his youth. Now, he thought, it was his turn to take care of them, help them feel less lonely. He had plans. Walking with them in Central Park. Watching the sun reflect on the surface of the Jersey Shore.

"They are older people, and I feel that I have little time left with them," said Fernandez-Garcia, choking back tears. "And maybe I'm not going to be there when they pass away."

At her home in New Jersey, Martha Piedra grieves for her great-nephew.

"I'm an old woman of 79 years with a whole lot of illnesses, so just imagine. What am I going to be able to do? I can't do anything," she says, her words dissolving into tears.

On the phone, his great-uncle's voice trembles. He remembers Fernandez-Garcia's cap and his calls from detention. He remembers the promises his grand-nephew made to gift it to him: a black baseball cap with a white Dodge Ram logo on it. Simple, but impossible to find elsewhere.

"I hope that he comes and brings it to me someday," says Díaz.

Piedra corrects him. "No, not someday. Please," she says. "Let it be soon."

The European Parliament voted Thursday to support adding Muslim Brotherhood-linked organizations and individuals to the European Union’s terrorist list, approving a sweeping resolution aimed at combating Islamist influence across Europe and preventing EU taxpayer funds from reaching extremist networks.

The resolution passed by a vote of 381-167, with 15 abstentions, calling on EU member states to develop a coordinated strategy to counter what lawmakers described as “Islamist entryism” and the influence of Muslim Brotherhood networks within European institutions and civil society.

The measure urges member states to provide information allowing the Council of the European Union to assess whether Brotherhood-linked individuals and organizations meet the criteria for terrorist designation. It also calls for scrutiny of alleged front organizations, financial networks, youth groups, and other entities associated with the movement.

Although the vote does not itself designate any organization as a terrorist group, it places political pressure on EU institutions and national governments to consider such action.

The resolution also calls on the European Commission to investigate whether EU funding has reached Brotherhood-associated organizations and to strengthen safeguards against public money being directed toward Islamist networks.

The initiative was spearheaded by the center-right European People’s Party (EPP), the Parliament’s largest political group, and drew support from conservative and centrist lawmakers.

Ahead of Thursday’s vote, French EPP lawmaker Céline Imart, who led the group’s efforts, called for a crackdown on Islamist influence while emphasizing the distinction between religious freedom and political extremism.

“We need to make sure Europe doesn’t fund Islamists. Islam as a faith and political Islam as an ideology must not be conflated. We must protect both democracy and religious freedom,” Imart said.

“Where rules allow, the Council should list individuals and organisations linked to the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist entities. European money must not fund groups that threaten our rights and freedoms,” she added.

The European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) Group, which also pushed for the measure, celebrated its passage.

“A massive victory for our hard work!” the group declared Thursday, describing its objective as “no funding, no collaboration and no more Muslim Brotherhood entryism in European institutions and Member States.”

The European Jewish Congress also welcomed the vote, calling it an important step toward confronting extremist networks and their financing while urging the Council to act on Parliament’s position.

The vote follows mounting scrutiny of the Brotherhood’s activities across Europe, including a May 2025 French government investigation that raised concerns about the movement’s alleged efforts to expand its influence through religious associations, educational institutions, and civil society organizations.

France’s National Assembly subsequently passed a resolution in January urging consideration of an EU terrorist designation.

The European Parliament’s vote follows similar action by President Donald Trump’s administration, which designated three Muslim Brotherhood chapters as terrorist entities in January after ordering a review of the movement’s branches in November.

The State Department designated the Lebanese Muslim Brotherhood as both a Foreign Terrorist Organization and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist, while the Treasury Department designated the Egyptian and Jordanian chapters as Specially Designated Global Terrorists, citing their support for Hamas.

“These designations reflect the opening actions of an ongoing, sustained effort to thwart Muslim Brotherhood chapters’ violence and destabilization wherever it occurs,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at the time.

The European Parliament’s resolution now leaves EU institutions and member states to determine whether to pursue similar designations and implement the proposed restrictions on funding and institutional cooperation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday fired Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander-in-chief of Ukraine's armed forces and named his replacement, following days of mass protests in Kyiv, the country's capital, and other cities nationwide demanding his removal.

It was the second major reversal Zelenskyy has made under street pressure, after protests last summer forced him to undo a law weakening Ukraine's anti-corruption watchdogs.

Zelenskyy appointed Mykhailo Drapatyi as the new army chief, according to a statement on social media.

"Our shared wish is one — victory over the enemy and conditions at the front and in pressure on Russia that would force Russia toward peace," Zelenskyy said.

The Ukrainian leader said he made the decision after a series of meetings with military commanders. They began shortly after protests broke out demanding the reinstatement of former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, seen by demonstrators as a driver of military modernization, and the removal of Syrskyi, who they said embodied the army's old, Soviet-style command culture.

Zelenskyy thanked Syrskyi for his achievements in Ukraine's fight against Russia and praised him for the defence of Kyiv and for operations in Kharkiv and Kursk.

"I am grateful to Oleksandr Syrskyi and to every one of our warriors for Ukraine's strong front-line positions," he said. "I am grateful to Mykhailo Drapatyi for holding that same view."

Drapatyi wrote in a Facebook post that serving Ukraine "has always been an honour for me, and during this war for independence, it means absolute responsibility." He thanked Syrskyi for his consistent work strengthening the Ukrainian military.

"I grew up in it," he said, referring to the army. "I will work responsibly, with focus and with respect for the people defending our state today."

Zelenskyy said Drapatyi and other commanders must present an updated defence strategy, including continued reform of the corps system, faster weapons and drone deliveries, stronger air defence against Russian strikes and a clearer mobilization plan.

Evhen, who goes by the call sign Lt. Stus, is a company commander in the 93rd Battalion stationed in the Donetsk region. He welcomed the announcement, saying much of the military has been waiting for the change.

"The new commander-in-chief inherits an army that is not in the best condition and whose morale is far from ideal," he told CBC News on Wednesday.

"One thing Syrskyi failed to do was stop constantly mixing brigades together — taking battalions from one brigade and attaching them to another. The corps system never really started functioning the way it was originally intended," Evhen said.

"That's probably the first challenge [Drapatyi] has to address."

He added that among the many issues that need to be addressed is exhaustion and burnout.

"When military personnel see that things are improving, their mental state will get better, and so will their resilience. War is war, and troops still have capacity left — I'm more than sure of that — but pushing things to extremes is undesirable," he said.

Zelenskyy met separately with Fedorov on Tuesday and offered him what he called a respected position in government that would unify the country's technology sector. It wasn't clear if Fedorov accepted the offer, or if the latest moves would satisfy protesters.

Fedorov congratulated Drapatyi, calling the appointment "new hope in the fight of free people for freedom and justice" and "a voice for change that could not go unheard."

Fedorov had criticized Syrskyi publicly before his dismissal, saying the general was blocking his reform efforts and needed to be replaced for Ukraine not to fail in its resistance against Russia.

He said Ukrainians' high expectations must now be met with a clear vision for ending the war, decisive action to preserve soldiers' lives, expand robotic warfare at the front, strike asymmetrically and exhaust Russia's economy.

Fedorov called Syrskyi to thank him for defending the Kyiv region, the Kharkiv operation and other battles, calling it "already an important part of Ukraine's history" but adding that the country must "move even faster and write new chapters, correcting all previous mistakes."

Is Ukraine running out of interceptors? | About That

The crisis began last Thursday, when Zelenskyy overhauled his wartime government, replacing his prime minister and firing Fedorov as defense minister after just six months in the post.

Zelenskyy cited an unworkable rift between Fedorov and Syrskyi, telling reporters that as the two couldn't resolve their dispute, he would "have to resolve it."

Following his dismissal, Fedorov publicly accused Syrskyi of blocking military reforms and fostering a top-down command culture, criticism that echoed complaints from soldiers and veterans over heavy casualties in costly front-line assaults.

The reshuffle immediately drew thousands of protesters into the streets of Kyiv and other cities, framing Fedorov's removal as Zelenskyy siding with an entrenched military old guard over a reformer.

The backlash promptly spread to the military: the Air Force's deputy commander resigned in protest, warning the move would weaken Ukraine's air defences; veterans and soldiers on leave joined the protests in Kyiv and other cities and numerous public figures among soldiers spoke out publicly against Syrskyi on social media.

Syrskyi has long been associated with a Soviet-style, top-down command culture, and many protesters said they wanted a new generation of generals who would place a higher priority on preserving soldiers' lives.

Within the military, Syrskyi has earned the gruesome nickname of "Butcher," which particularly spread during his command of the defence of Bakhmut, one of the war's longest and costliest battles.

Syrskyi became the army's commander in chief in February 2024, replacing Gen. Valerii Zaluzhnyi, who subsequently became Ukraine's Ambassador to the United Kingdom.

Zelenskyy did not mention any new post for Syrskyi, saying he had discussed the four-star-general's future service with him.

Ukraine has been in a state of all-out war with Russia for more than four years, after Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022.
