An up-and-coming UK rapper's thanked Linkin Park's Mike Shinoda for "changing my life" after he praised one of her freestyles.

Morgan Da Savage's rap went viral after she performed on DJ and producer Toddla T's independent music platform Steeze Factory.

Shinoda mentioned her name when asked by BBC News at Download Festival who he'd want to collaborate with on a 2026 version of Collision Course, their 2004 mash-up album with Jay-Z.

Da Savage says it feels "surreal" as she listened to Linkin Park growing up and all the attention means her song Innit is going to be released next week.

Linkin Park became the first female-fronted band to headline the UK's biggest rock festival last weekend.

Speaking to the BBC at Download, Shinoda said it was "refreshing" to see Da Savage's rap and he immediately showed it to his bandmates.

"She was going crazy. Whatever's happening over here [in the UK] is cool, it's fresh, it's got motion," he said.

When BBC Newsbeat caught up with Da Savage, she says she cried when she found out about the clip through a message on social media.

"Linkin Park have gone on the FYP and they see me," the 21-year-old says.

"It's unbelievable, I'm just so grateful to him to even say my name.

"I was like 'no way, he knows my name'. He could have said anybody and he's gone Morgan Da Savage.

"It just shows like what a real person he is even to do that for me. It's changed my life."

Shinoda spotted Da Savage's rap in a cypher on Steeze Factory's Instagram, where it was also praised by Rizzle Kicks' Jordan Stephens.

The project was set up by former BBC Radio 1 and 1Xtra DJ Toddla T, who's married to DJ Annie Mac, to highlight UK talent.

It's featured bigger acts like Aitch, Window Kid and legendary grime crew Roll Deep - while also giving space for up-and-coming artists like Da Savage.

A report from Seed Sounds Weekender, backed up by artists including Matty Healy from The 1975, suggested more than 1.5 million 18-25s may have given up live music ambitions because of the disappearance of pubs and music venues.

"It's just what the scene needs right now," Morgan says about Steeze Factory.

"It's not just famous artists that have blown [up], it's all underground artists that are actually getting known from it."

The rapper's also full of praise for people like Toddla T, as well as DJs AG and Mak10 who put on street sets that often go viral.

"They're making it easier access for artists to get on to that," she says.

"When you start, it's very hard as an artist. It's really good for upcoming artists now that they can show themselves."

In his interview at Download, Shinoda said he'd been drawn to emerging UK talent, even performers who didn't have a huge fanbase yet like Da Savage.

"Some of them have huge followings, some have tiny followings, but it's interesting to me," he says.

But despite the praise, Shinoda was clear a collaboration with Da Savage isn't on the cards - at least not yet.

"Let's not go overboard and say do a Collision Course, that's not going to happen at this point."

But Da Savage tells Newsbeat she'd love to collaborate with the band, having grown up listening to the mix of rock and rap on tracks like Numb/Encore.

She says she's sent Shinoda a DM and has a message for the Linkin Park star.

"It means a lot. You're a real person. You've inspired my life."

More than 1,500 pounds of ready-to-eat pork shipped to New York, New Jersey, and six other states have been recalled at the US Department of Agriculture’s “highest warning” level due to Listeria concerns.

Two US-based companies — Prime Line Distributors, Inc. based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Ferrarini USA, Inc, based in Hoboken — have recalled 1,513 pounds of imported ready-to-eat pork guanciale that may be “adulterated with Listeria monocytogenes,” the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service announced on Sunday.

The recall, classified as a “Class I” recall, is the USDA’s highest warning level involving “high or medium risk.”

The problem was revealed during a routine import reinspection when a product sample tested positive for Listeria monocytogenes.

No one has been sickened due to consuming the pork thus far, the FSIS said in a statement.

Prime Line Distributors Inc. has recalled various weight cardboard cases containing two pieces of individually vacuum-packed “Prime Line Distributors, Inc. Guanciale Pork Jowl Product of Italy” items with a best if used by date of May 16, 2027, and the lot number 263311US.

The Sunshine State company also recalled various individually vacuum-sealed packages of “Guanciale Pork Jowl Product of Italy” items with the same lot number and expiration date, bearing an additional “Dok Guanciale” label on the packaging.

Ferranin USA, Inc. recalled various weights of cardboard cases containing two pieces of individually vacuum-packed “Guanciale Pork Jowl Product of Italy” and various weights of individually vacuum-packed “Ferrarini Guanciale Dry-Cured Pork Jowl” —  both with the same best if used by date of May 16, 2027, and the lot number 263311US.

The slew of possibly contaminated meat bears the establishment number “IT 1937 L CE” inside the Italian mark of inspection or printed on the case label.

Prime Line Distributors, Inc, items were shipped to food service and retail locations in Florida, and Ferrarini USA, Inc., items were shipped to distributors and food service locations in California, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey, New York and Texas, officials said.

“FSIS is concerned that some products may be in food service and retail refrigerators and freezers,” the FSIS wrote, urging companies “not to serve or sell these products.”

Consuming food contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes can cause listeriosis, a serious infection that primarily affects older adults, people with weakened immune systems, pregnant women, and their newborns.

The illness — which can be treated with antibiotics — can cause fever, muscle aches, headache, stiff neck, confusion, loss of balance, and convulsions, sometimes after diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms.

In pregnant women, the infection can cause miscarriages, stillbirths, premature delivery, or life-threatening infection of the newborn.

Serious and sometimes fatal infections are also possible in older adults and persons with weakened immune systems.

Kerry Hodgetts says he has nobody to pass his trade onto when he retires. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

There is a shortage of locksmiths in Australia, despite $40,000 on offer from governments to cover training costs in Tasmania.

It calls into question which other artisan trades are falling by the wayside and which are thriving.

Tasmania's heritage homes require maintenance that may not be on offer in the future, with the next generation increasingly uninterested in picking up artisan skills.

Kerry Hodgetts loves his job as a locksmith, but acknowledged that the future of his industry faces challenges.

Over his two decades in business, Mr Hodgetts has taken on seven or eight apprentices, with only one seeing the apprenticeship to completion.

Locksmith Kerry Hodgetts worries his industry is dying. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Hodgetts, from Launceston, in northern Tasmania, said traditional lock-smithing could fade into obscurity as people turn more to electronic security for their homes and businesses.

In April, the peak locksmith body in Australia made a national recruitment call-out, appealing to anyone looking for a new line of work — particularly women and school leavers.

The head of the national lock-smithing body labelled the traditional craft a boutique industry that is '"almost invisible" and not front of mind when people are considering a trade.

"We need thousands of people in our industry across Australia," Master Locksmiths Association's Martin Coote said.

Lock-smithing is "almost invisible" to those considering trades, according to the Master Locksmiths Association. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

With the $30,000 TAFE course fully subsidised by the government and a $10,000 sweetener sign-on bonus, all the stops are being pulled out in the hope the industry does not fall by the wayside.

However, the trade cannot be fully completed from Tasmania, with training blocks on the mainland required to complete the apprenticeship. Cost is also a major barrier for many.

Locksmith apprentices who complete their studies are hard to come by. (Supplied: Master Locksmiths Association)

It is not the only artisan craft needing new blood in Tasmania.

Louise Ridge has been in the lead-lighting business for more than three decades and is almost ready to hang up the tools.

Louise Ridge said her profession is "in vogue" currently. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

She is one of a handful of people left with the knowledge to undertake essential maintenance on buildings like churches, some of which have windows fused together well over 100 years ago.

"It's just a shame people aren't taking it up," Ms Ridge said.

Stained glass artist of three decades Louise Ridge works from a small studio in the town of Spreyton, northern Tasmania. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Ms Ridge said stained glass art had been back in demand lately, and she was busier than ever.

"People love it, it's in vogue and I think they realise it's a dying art and then it's going be harder and harder to get done," she said.

With the materials required slowly getting phased out due to lack of demand, Ms Ridge can see the writing on the wall for the craft, but is proud of the legacy she will leave.

"I like knowing that my work's going to outlive me, and it's going last for another 100 years after I've gone," she said.

A career counsellor said young people today are less likely to pick a specialty and stick with it for a career. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Simon Martin's leather whips are in high demand and have been ordered by the likes of Hollywood stars, are framed in state and federal parliamentary offices and adorn the belts of the country's best rodeo stars.

COVID forced the business, in Spreyton in Tasmania's north, to get online and ship internationally — and it paid off.

Leather crafter Simon Martin ships his products around the world. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

He has trained five apprentices during his two decades in business — now qualified, they make up the bulk of his production staff.

Although like lock-smithing, it is not something that can be taught locally, with apprentices completing their qualification via an interstate institution with representatives who visit Tasmania.

A 20-foot bull whip made from kangaroo leather takes three weeks to make and the wait to buy one is currently three years.

It will also set you back around $3,000.

Simon Martin has trained five apprentices in his trade, all of whom stuck with it. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

It is a lucrative market in a niche field that the next generation are keen to get into.

Seventeen-year-old Tom Hill grew up on a farm in nearby Ulverstone and is 18 months into a five-year apprenticeship in certificate three and four in leather-making.

"It's very cool … there's not many people that have got the chance to have a go at it," he said.

Tom Hill is 18 months into a five year apprenticeship at Simon Martin Leathercraft and Whips. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The Beacon Foundation is a Tasmanian not-for-profit that works with school-aged children as they embark on their career journey and first work experience.

Strategic partnerships manager Ebony Bridle says young people will have multiple careers in their lifetime, unlike their parents before them, who were more likely to stick with one job, company or role.

Ebony Bridle is the strategic partnerships manager at the Beacon Foundation in Tasmania. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

"A really important message that a young person can hear is that a career path is not going to be a linear process," she said.

Mrs Bridle said students would usually only "be what they can see" — such as more common apprenticeship roles like builders and electricians.

"We know there's a really strong workforce demand for trades and allied trades," she said.

Ms Bridle said young people were more likely to have "varied careers" across different professions. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

With a varied career ahead for the next generation, she said core skills were essential as they transitioned through different roles.

"If they're not sure what they want to do, having that sense of self-awareness and knowing their strengths and interests — that the first part-time job or entry-level job for them is really important," she said.

"Because that's where they're building those transferable skills that will lead them to that next opportunity."

The summer of sewer diving keeps on going.

Five “mole people” dove down a manhole into the Long Island drainage system in an overnight run Thursday — just one week after a seemingly separate trio emerged in NYC.

The unidentified urban spelunkers descended into the Wantagh storm drain at the intersection of Wantagh Avenue and Jerusalem Avenue at around 1 a.m., WABC reported.

The group was captured on surveillance cameras working together to get the cover open before sliding into the opening into the underground in a matter of seconds, according to video obtained by the outlet.

The men, wearing black shirts and shorts, slipped inside before closing the cover as all five vanished into the depths below the street, where several shopping centers are located.

Two witnesses had watched the night crawlers and called the Nassau County Police, the outlet reported.

Investigators went down into the sewer but came up empty-handed in their search for the wannabe Ninja Turtles.

Residents of the Long Island neighborhood questioned the potential motives behind the midnight adventures.

“It’s kind of dangerous; I don’t know what they have in mind,” one resident told the outlet.

“There’s a level of concern, but you can’t stop people from doing what they want to do,” a man said.

“It’s kind of crazy to be honest with you. I have seen it on the news recently,” a third added.

Thursday’s sewer break-in comes a week after a trio was seen climbing up from a manhole outside Penn Station and Madison Square Garden in Manhattan around 4:20 a.m. on Aug. 18.

The viral TikTok video captured the headlamp-wearing men emerging from underground near the intersection of 32nd Street and Seventh Avenue — just feet from the main entrance to Penn Station.

The trio has not been captured, officials said.

NYPD detectives were using surveillance footage and facial recognition technology to try to identify and track the men down.

The Big Apple has had several reports of large groups of men entering or emerging from the city’s sewage systems, including in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, back in May.

Authorities cautioned against the bizarre adventure, warning potential divers of the dangers in the sewage system.

“Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks, and confined spaces,” the DEP said in a statement. “For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole, or outfall.”

Officials believe the NYC incidents may have involved migrants searching for valuables lost underneath the big city, WABC reported.
lord-timpson-resignation:
Lord James Timpson's appointment was praised as pioneering

The prisons minister has resigned from the government, the BBC has been told.

Lord James Timpson was appointed to the role in July 2024 after leaving his job as CEO of the Timpson group, a business which provides key cutting and shoe repair services and employs hundreds of former prisoners.

His arrival in government was greeted with much fanfare by some in the Labour Party and described as "radical" and "innovative".

But in a departing statement on Monday, seen exclusively by the BBC, Lord Timpson said he was stepping down and it was an "honour" to serve in the post.

His statement did not give a specific reason for resigning, but it is understood he feels he has done as much as he can in the role.

Prisons in England and Wales were at crisis point, reaching almost full capacity, when he first entered Sir Keir Starmer's government.

He oversaw the controversial early release scheme which saw tens of thousands of inmates let out to create more space in jails.

His critics will argue prisons continue to be violent, drug infused and overcrowded, while probation officers still report being overworked and unable to cope.

But figures do show assaults against staff and self-harm in prisons are falling.

Lord Timpson said in his resignation statement that he had left "our prisons and probation service in a much healthier and happier state than two years ago".

He added: "I'm proud to have become the longest-serving minister in this role for 15 years. I'm also proud that 75% of prisons and 90% of probation teams are now performing better than when I started.

"Self-harm, violence and assaults on staff are all down, and fewer people are leaving prison without a home to go to, a measure of dignity I care about deeply."

He also pointed to the Women's Justice Board he established, saying he "believe[s] most women should not be in prison at all" and "diverting them away from custody, helping them with often chaotic, damaged, and addicted lives, is one of the changes I'm proud to have achieved".

His critics may question why he is leaving before the Sentencing Act 2026 is enacted in September, when more people are expected to be released early and further criminals will serve their sentences in the community.

A source in the Ministry of Justice told the BBC: "We're gutted he's going but the new person is going to have their work cut out to get their head round what's round the corner."

Louis Theroux’s The Settlers, which examines the Israeli settler movement in the occupied West Bank and its ambitions for Gaza, has been nominated for an International Emmy Award.

The British documentary, produced by Mindhouse Productions, was named on Wednesday among four contenders for the documentary prize at the 54th International Emmy Awards. It is up against programmes from Mexico, Singapore and France.

Filmed in Israel and the occupied West Bank in 2024, The Settlers marks Theroux’s return to a subject he explored in his 2011 documentary The Ultra Zionists. The film follows the British-American journalist as he speaks to Palestinians, Israeli settlers and Israeli activists opposed to settlement expansion.

The Settlers review: Louis Theroux's urgent documentary lays bare plans for Gaza

Among its central subjects is Daniella Weiss, a veteran leader of the settler movement, who tells Theroux of her desire to establish Israeli settlements in Gaza. The film also follows settlers attempting to establish outposts in the occupied West Bank and examines how such communities can grow before eventually receiving formal recognition from the Israeli authorities.

The National's five-star review describes the documentary as “fearless journalism”, with Theroux’s restrained interview style allowing his subjects to lay out their positions at length.

Also nominated is Exposure: Breaking Ranks: Inside Israel’s War, produced by Zandland for ITV1. The investigative documentary is competing in the current affairs category.

The documentary features interviews with Israeli military conscripts, reservists and veterans who served in Gaza. According to ITV, their testimony includes allegations of indiscriminate bombardment, the use of human shields and the shooting of civilians, raising questions about possible breaches of international law.

Qatar is the only Arab country represented among the 22 countries with nominated programmes this year. Al Jazeera Arabic’s Missing in Gaza is nominated in the news category, alongside programmes from Brazil, Portugal and the UK.

Al Jazeera English also received a nomination in current affairs for Al Jazeera Investigates: Hasina: 36 Days in July, which examines the political upheaval in Bangladesh.

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

By James Tugwell

ABC North Qld

Topic:Conservation

Mahogany gliders live in forests along a small stretch of coastline north of Townsville. (Supplied: Daryl Dickson)

Nobody knows for sure how many endangered mahogany gliders, which "disappeared from science" for a century, still exist in their little pocket on the North Queensland coastline.

That is half the problem; the other half is that there is no funding to find out.

The small gliders are an example of the fight endangered-animal support groups face for funding and how a disaster can sometimes lead to a moment of fame.

The mahogany glider is one of Australia's largest tree-dwelling gliders and lives in a 120-kilometre-long stretch of eucalypt forest north of Townsville.

It was discovered in 1883 but never classified in the Queensland Museum.

"It then disappeared from science for over 100 years. The specimen was just filed away," former chair of the national mahogany glider recovery team Daryl Dickson said.

The mahogany glider was declared a unique species in 1993. (Supplied: Daryl Dickson)

In 1993, it was rediscovered in North Queensland and declared a unique species with the name Petaurus gracilis, meaning graceful rope dancer.

At the same time, it was declared endangered with more than 60 per cent of its habitat already cleared.

That habitat was further decimated by Cyclone Yasi in 2011, which at the time was the worst storm to hit Queensland.

"Cyclone Yasi was a game changer for us," Ms Dickson said.

"We managed to get into the limelight for a little while."

Daryl Dickson says funding for the species boomed after Cyclone Yasi. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

There was an influx of funding and the recovery team worked towards a scientific recovery plan for the species.

But then Ms Dickson said the funding ran out, which left the recovery team "in limbo". The finalised plan was shelved.

The recent Keeping Country Connected for Mahogany Gliders project, funded by the Queensland government, ended this month.

There is funding for ecosystem-wide action such as removing weeds or building road crossings.

"We've had our moment in the sun."

And that came when she felt the group was on the verge of a breakthrough.

Ms Dickson said the team was "always guessing" when it came to population numbers and locations, information that is crucial for analysing long-term changes.

Daryl Dickson says drone technology could help monitor mahogany gliders into the future, if there was funding. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

A researcher recently flew a thermal drone over mahogany glider habitat, revealing an easy and accurate way to monitor the population.

From one brief night's flying, she estimated the population was about 3,000.

Ms Dickson said the "hugely expensive" drones "could be the answer for the future". But there was no funding.

"If we had a regular monitoring process, at least we'd see the warning signs early enough to perhaps be able to make enough noise to make the government pay attention," she said.

"It's frustrating to see things that could be done but that we have no capacity to do."

Daryl Dickson says there is no funding available for projects specific to the mahogany glider. (Supplied: Daryl Dickson)

More than 15 years after Cyclone Yasi, Ms Dickson said the mahogany glider had lost the political attention that secured funding.

"At the moment, the limelight is pointing at other species. We have so many endangered species with no basic funding," she said.

"Around Australia, there are so many amazing species that are all 'pick me, pick me' and there are so many brilliant groups working for these animals.

"We're all fighting the same battles. It's sad we're fighting against each other, but it's difficult days for government and conservation."

An endangered North Queensland flying possum gets a stepping stone to recovery under a program to help with its habitat pathways.

There are more than 2,100 plants and animals threatened with extinction in Australia.

Australian Threatened Species commissioner Fiona Fraser said they were all vying for a share of funding from different levels of government and various sectors and organisations.

For example, she said the Australian government had committed more than $800 million since 2022, guided by the threatened species action plan, which prioritises 110 species and 20 landscapes for a focused effort.

"Our threatened species definitely need more love. They need more resources. They need more science.

"So, making decisions about funding is super important."

Fiona Fraser says threatened species can always do with more funding and support. (Supplied: DCCEEW)

Dr Fraser said funding often prioritised wide-scale environmental action that benefited many animals rather than focusing on individual species.

"Some species need a very bespoke approach … whereas other species require landscape action to mitigate threats," she said.

Dr Fraser said some iconic species, for example the koala in Queensland, often received more funding because of their relative fame.

But she said that was a good thing because "actions to improve koala habitat … actually benefit the many, many other species that co-occur with koalas".

Meanwhile, Ms Dickson was determined to keep the recovery team in contact, even without a chairperson, funding or regular meetings.

"We just need to keep going until such time that, perhaps, the spotlight shines on the mahogany glider again."

mandatory-sex-ed:
Relationships and sex education for 16 to 18-year-olds could be made mandatory in a bid to prevent violence against women and girls.

The Labour MP for Hitchin, Alistair Strathern, has been pressing the government for change and pledged to end a postcode lottery of provision for teenagers in further education, with the introduction of his private member's bill.

He said his draft law would extend the time school pupils are taught how to navigate complex issues in relationships and recognise coercive control and other forms of abuse.

"For too long, children in further education have missed out because of gaps in provision of relationships and sex education," Strathern said.

Strathern was drawn 14th in the private members' bills ballot. His draft legislation is due to be debated during Friday sittings in Parliament.

The MP, who is also co-chair of the Labour group for men and boys, continued: "At a time when the worst corners of the internet are preying on teenagers, with their own harmful takes on what makes a healthy relationship, we surely owe young people far better than this."

He said he hoped the bill would make it mandatory for all settings to give children space, support and advice.

"With 16 to 19-year-olds facing the highest rates of domestic abuse of any age group, the real-world consequences of failing to act couldn't be clearer," he added.

"Young people's exposure to extreme content online makes this legislation more important than ever."

The Relationships and Sex Education (Further Education Sector) Bill follows a petition by the survivor-led campaign group Make it Mandatory, which called for sex education to be mandated to 18 and gathered more than 106,000.

Faustine Petron, founder of Make it Mandatory, said: "As someone who experienced an abusive relationship I know how important such a change could be.

"We now need government to honour its commitment to me and the bereaved families who support this campaign by taking it forward and ensuring it becomes law, as we know all too well that it has the potential to change and save lives."

End Violence Against Women Coalition and the Sex Education Forum also welcomed the introduction of the Bill.

Lucy Emmerson, chief executive at the Sex Education Forum, said: "It makes complete sense to extend relationships and sex education to further education because this is the time when many young people will be starting their first romantic and sexual relationships.

"Having reliable information about healthy relationships provided by trusted adults is proven to help prevent harm.

"There is overwhelming support for mandating RSE [Relationship Sex Education] up to 18 years old, and this move is backed by leaders in education, safeguarding, health and wellbeing and by colleges and young people themselves."

marineland_beluga_rescue:
The U.S. government has formally approved an emergency rescue of most of the beluga whales from Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., to aquariums in the United States.

Moving the whales from the once-popular theme park a few kilometres from the Horseshoe Falls to the American aquariums is expected to take some weeks and still involves some steps including clearance by Canadian veterinarians for the whales to travel.

The Department of Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) recently endorsed a rescue plan for the 30 belugas still living at the theme park closed to the public in 2024, which would see the whales split up and sent to Oceanogràfic València in Spain or one of four U.S. locations: Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and two SeaWorld facilities in San Diego, Calif., and San Antonio, Texas.

Johnny Ford, vice-president of communications for Shedd Aquarium, told CBC on Wednesday that under the current plan 28 of the belugas will be taken to the American aquariums, with two other whales bound for Spain.

The Spanish aquarium is still awaiting the necessary permits from the Spanish government, the American aquarium collective said in a statement Wednesday.

The group said Marineland is in a "financial crisis and is no longer willing or able to continue their [whales'] care."

Marineland said it welcomed the U.S. authorization of the relocation. "We recognize we can no longer provide the long-term care these animals require, and we believe this rescue. . .is in the whales' best interest," Marineland said.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration authorized the emergency rescue, sending the whales to the aquariums in the U.S. that are all accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums.

DFO Minister Joanne Thompson said in a statement on Wednesday that the approval "is an encouraging and critical next step for the safe relocation of the whales."

Permits from The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITIES) needed to take the whales out of the country have been issued, and as a condition of approving the export permits a health check for each animal must be completed by a Canadian veterinarian, Thompson said.

"Once this step has been completed and all appropriate documentation has been provided to Fisheries and Oceans Canada, I will provide the final Fisheries Act authorizations to enable the relocation," she said.

The latest milestone means dedicated care staff from the U.S. aquariums will soon arrive at Marineland to assess the whales' well-being and make preparations for travel, the American consortium said.

"Once the belugas are cleared for travel by Canadian veterinarians, aquarium experts will accompany the animals to their new homes, where they will be met with diverse seafood to meet their nutritional needs, high quality environments with guaranteed water quality and onsite medical care should they require it at any time," their statement said.

"This rescue effort will take several weeks to mobilize and complete, and the comfort and safety of the whales remains of the utmost importance," the statement read. "Details will continue to change as this process moves forward, but the aquariums are committed to providing accurate updates along the way."

Last January, CBC News reported that Marineland was threatening to euthanize the 30 belugas and four dolphins unless Canada granted permission to ship them to the United States.

That came after the DFO last fall denied Marineland's request to export its belugas to a theme park in China.

Fate of remaining deer, elk at closed Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., still uncertain

Federal government denies Marineland request to export belugas

In a statement at the time, Thompson said she could not in good conscience approve the export to China and that her decision aligned with regulations in the Fisheries Act to protect marine mammals from exploitation.

To approve the request would have meant a continued life in captivity and a return to public entertainment, Thompson said.

By Simon Smale

Topic:Swimming

Wed 10 Jun 2026 at 8:14am

Cameron McEvoy has got into the habit of making the incredible look relatively routine.

So much so that his undoubtedly incredible 50m freestyle world record set earlier this year at the China Open was only the beginning of what he feels he can achieve.

"I definitely think I can get faster," McEvoy said upon his return from China.

The statement seems both scarcely believable yet utterly convincing when coming from the 32-year-old defending Olympic champion. And it makes the event at this evening's Australian swimming trials a must-watch.

Especially because the Sydney Olympic venue is something of a "fast" pool.

Need proof? There have been 37 long-course world records set in the Sydney Olympic pool since it opened in 1994.

The men's 50-metre freestyle world record has been broken three times at Homebush, all by a super suit-clad Eamon Sullivan in that early autumn of accelerated development in 2008.

That being said, just one of those 37 marks set in Sydney still stands: Kaylee McKeown's 200m back.

Budapest's Danube Arena and Fukuoka's competition pool have six current world records each.

Cam McEvoy holds the 50m freestyle world record, but he thinks he can go faster. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Can McEvoy return the men's 50m free to the honour roll tonight?

"On paper, there's definitely room to improve," McEvoy said.

"Whether that happens on an execution point of view, I can't be so certain.

"Even on the training side of things, I'm constantly refining it and developing it.

"The underlying skeleton is always the same, but the actual day-to-day representation of what that looks like; there's many different forms that can take.

"So a part of the game is just rolling the dice on a new approach every season and seeing what comes with that too, which is really exciting and gives a lot more purpose than just chasing times and medals as well.

"So there's a lot more to do."

Eamon Sullivan broke the 50m free world record three times in the space of a couple of months at the start of the super-suit era. (AAP Photo: Jenny Evans)

Prior to McEvoy's staggering swim in Shenzhen, the 50m free record had remained a somewhat unattainable target.

At 16 years, it was one of the longest-standing world records remaining in swimming, one of the last relics of the super-suit era — a time both set in the distant past and an inaccessible technology-fuelled future.

Australian swimmer and 50m freestyle world record holder Cam McEvoy says it is "ludicrous" that doped-up swimmers are being offered as much as $2 million to break a world record, while his legitimate mark earned him nothing.

Prior to the technological arms race that overtook swimsuit manufacture in the late 2000s, the 50m world record had only been beaten four times in the 19 years since Matt Biondi set his mark of 22.14 at the Seoul Olympics in 1988.

American Tom Jager bettered it three times before Russia's Alexander Popov, the very definition of the anti-super suit swimmer, achieved a mark of 21.64 in speedo briefs and without wearing a swim cap in Moscow in 2000.

However, from the outset of the super-suit era, that all changed.

In February 17, 2008, Australian Eamon Sullivan set a new record of 21.56 at Homebush in the Australian Championships.

By the time César Cielo blasted a 20.91 down the pool just 23 months later, the record had been bettered five times by swimmers wearing suits that covered their torsos and extended down to their ankles.

It had taken 19 years for swimmers to take 0.5 seconds off the record before the super suit era. During it, 0.73 seconds had been erased in under two years.

César Cielo held the 50m free world record for 16 years. (Getty Images: Clive Rose)

Progress can be achieved in a number of different ways.

Technologically, as was certainly the case in the late 2000's; nefariously, as was the case at the farcical Enhanced Games; or through some other form of innovation, perhaps through training specification.

It's training innovation that is precisely what McEvoy has employed to get himself into shape specifically for 50-metre racing.

McEvoy's approach is not necessarily new. British short course specialist Mark Foster was prioritising a less-is-more training regime as long as 30 years ago to great effect: the six-time short course world champion broke the 50m freestyle world record four times and the 50m butterfly five times in a 25-metre pool during his stellar career.

Ben Proud (right) who Cam McEvoy (left) beat to Olympic gold in Paris, has taken the Enhanced route forward, eliminating himself from legitimate competition. (Getty Images: VCG)

But McEvoy has taken things to the nth degree, exploring how he can tailor his training even more specifically.

"There's a lot of different ways, from a day-to-day perspective, that this training can go," McEvoy explained when asked whether he was surprised that it had taken him so long under his new regime to break the record.

"Because it'd never been done before, I had to be the guinea pig to trial these out.

"The past four seasons, I had done something, I got a result, but then there was other stuff that I hadn't yet exposed myself to that I wanted to just at least see what would happen if I did.

"I spent the first four seasons pivoting and doing, on the surface, rather different stuff just to gather as much information as I could.

"Off the back of the world championships last year, I'd got to a point where I'd learnt enough and I could really put together something that put all of the good qualities from all of those approaches into one singular one, which is what I've done and it's paid off.

"Surprisingly, it's a little bit more leaning into the extreme side of things, even with respect to what I've already been doing."

Cameron McEvoy is an Olympic champion in the 50m free. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

What does McEvoy mean by that?

"So, before China Open, I hadn't done any rep past 25 metres," McEvoy said.

"I've been in a strength and power block, a lot of my energy had been around protecting that type of stimulus.

"So in the water, it was all 25 metres.

"If you take the dive out, my first stroke set after 10 [metres], really I only go on 15 metres of swimming in one go with 10-plus minutes' rest in between each rep."

That lack of metres is an anathema to most traditional ways of swim coaching, where yardage is king and disciples were sent ploughing up and down the pool on repeat for hours at a time, racking up 70km a week.

McEvoy would barely cover those sorts of distances in an entire year now.

Less is most definitely leading to more for Cam McEvoy. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"I'd be lucky to go over one-and-a-half kilometres a week in the water, over anywhere between two to four sessions," McEvoy said.

"The rest of the time is spent in the gym working on mobility, working on general strength and power — which is a stark contrast to my 30 to 70 kilometres a week that I've done traditionally in the past.

"They were for a spread of events, but I've always been a sprinter. It's very, very different."

Does that not affect his sprint endurance? Perhaps. McEvoy admitted that the final 10 metres of his record-breaking 50 was a fair bit harder than the first half of the race.

"There was a stark contrast in how amazing the first 30 metres felt and how much of a fight the last 10 metres was," he noted with a grin.

But when you're already travelling so fast, that speed from the first half of the race carried him through nicely.

Impressively, if McEvoy can continue to hone his approach and refine the most out of his body, there could be an expectation that he will break the record every time he gets in the water.

Cam McEvoy has been blazing a trail for sprinters across the world. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

As much success that McEvoy has enjoyed by swimming less, Australian Dolphins head coach Rohan Taylor noted that his low-distance approach would only work with certain caveats.

"I think there does need to be looking into what is enough, but also where are they in their swimming journey," Taylor said.

"Cam's one of the best … he's our Australian record holder in the 100 [freestyle], he is world-class in the 200 free, and so he has that background and he's technically really, really superior.

"I think that adds to what he's doing, and so it's the right time for him.

"The jury's out on whether a young kid can come in and start training from that perspective and get to where he [Cam] is."

Taylor's note of caution is important. What McEvoy is doing is not a short cut, but a fine-tuning of an already elite swimmer. After all, McEvoy is the Australian record holder over 100m freestyle, with his time of 47.04 set all the way back at the 2016 Australian Championships in Adelaide.

"I think there's an amount of aquatic fitness you need to get with your technique to be able to sustain the type of training loads that you need," Taylor continued.

"I'm not a physiologist and a bio-mechanist from that point of view, but from my own coaching experience, there's garbage yardage and then there's specificity.

"So what's the specificity you need to do? With a young athlete, you want to develop their technique so it's sound and it's conditioned and it can hold up.

"But I would encourage exploration. I think we want to explore what we can do if we just keep sticking to the same old things with the same results.

Rohan Taylor is excited about what Cam McEvoy can do, but notes it's not for everyone. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"The old philosophy that my mentor told me is if you're going to play a piano and be a concert pianist, you don't practise the trumpet, you practise the piano as often as you can and be an expert at it. And I think this is a perfect example of that.

"To be honest, that's the kind of stuff that goes into some of our best swimmers in the world when there are events, whether it's a 50 all the way up to 1,500, they're really specific about the work they do and do exactly what they need to do.

"I think what we're seeing here is something special."

ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

McEvoy himself said he understood what he needed to achieve through every single metre of a one-lap dash: "I'd say I am hyper-specific," he said.

"I've spent a lot of time understanding basically every metre of a 50 metres, what goes into it, how the body responds at that point in time and basically trying to transform that into some form of training stimulus.

"Hyper-specificity is really what I've been doing."

His innovative, counter-intuitive training regime has sparked a revision of everything that swimmers and coaches thought they knew.

"'You never change things by fighting the existing reality," wrote the man whose record he took, Brazilian sprinter César Cielo, when congratulating McEvoy on the record.

"'To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete."

McEvoy has built that model and now he's refined it, is looking to see just how far — and fast — he can take it.

A California car fanatic and a Hooters calendar girl from Florida had been on a first date when they died in a horrific fireball crash, her family has revealed.

James Wehr, 27, and Alexis “Lexi” Kramer, 22, were killed around 12:20 a.m. Sunday when his 2019 McLaren slammed into a tree in Irvine, Orange County. The massive force of the impact split the supercar in two and saw it burst into flames, killing both people inside, with harrowing video showing the extent of the damage.

A member of Kramer’s family told the California Post that Wehr paid for her to fly from her home in Lakeland, Fla., to California Friday to meet for the first time after one month of chatting on social media.

The family member said Wehr had told Kramer he was separated from his wife Emma and they were finalizing their divorce, but it had not been filed with the courts in Orange County. The relative said Kramer believed she was traveling to see a man who loved her. The pair then spent all of Saturday together.

Wehr first took Kramer out to breakfast before the pair headed to Nobu for dinner and later drinks at the Pendry, the relative said.

A photograph posted to Wehr’s social media account before the crash showed his flashy supercar parked outside the hotel Saturday night.

The family member said: “He talked to her every day, all the time and finally got her to fly out to California to come see him.”

Kramer had never met Wehr in person before making the trip. The pair had met through Instagram direct messages and had been talking for about a month, according to the relative. She knew Wehr was married but believed his assurances that the relationship was effectively over. “She only knew from what he told her that they were almost done finalizing their divorce,” the family member said.

The relative said they had warned Kramer about being skeptical Wehr was actually getting divorced, but that Kramer wanted to believe him: “She tried so hard to give him the benefit of the doubt because I was wary about if he was actually getting divorced.”

On the night of the crash, Kramer sent a photo to a family member from breakfast with a message reading, “At cute breakfast place.”

The picture showed the side profile of a man whose tattoo sleeve matched Wehr’s.

Hours later, the McLaren was stopped at a red light before accelerating at a high rate of speed when the light turned green, police said.

The driver lost control, crossed a curb and slammed into a tree. Authorities have not said who was driving or released a precise speed as the investigation continues.

The Post has reached out to Wehr’s family and business for comment.

Mechanical pencils have so many uses in the workplace. People use pencils every day to calculate payroll, write letters, and complete their work. Students especially use them in schools to do their homework and get good grades.

While much of the world has moved towards digital format, mechanical pencils make writing and design easier than ever before.

Mechanical Pencil Day celebrates the history of these pencils and encourages people to celebrate mechanical pencils and their many uses in our daily lives.

Celebrate Mechanical Pencil Day by reading up on the inventors of these fantastic pencils. Read up on the story of different companies such as BIC, Paper-mate, and Pentel.

Take the time today to use mechanical pencils in whatever field of work you do. Give out pencils to your local schools for free and help students get through their schools easier.

Also, give them out to your friends and family, tell your friends and family members about this holiday and educate them about the history of mechanical pencils.

Pencils were created around the time that graphite deposits were being discovered in Europe during the early 16th century.

The first primitive design of the pencil was invented in 1565 by Conrad Gesner, a naturalist, and bibliographer from Switzerland. These pencils were graphite sticks wrapped in string and later were designed with wood so it could be sharpened.

The first mechanical pencil that had tools to move the lead instead of manually sharpening the lead was patented in 1822 by Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins in Britain. From there, multiple companies began to begin mass producing mechanical pencils.

Mechanical pencils now operate by three types of methods; rachet-based, clutch-based, and screw-based. Today, mechanical pencils have different varieties of lead width and have multiple frames, including plastic, metal, and wood. These pencils are used for writing, but can also be used for art and design.

Due to the slick nature of the mechanical pencil, people now have the ability to create fine details and don’t have to use a pencil sharper. Mechanical Pencil Day celebrates the history of mechanical pencils and how it is today used in workplaces and schools all over the world.

People celebrate the holiday by collecting antique mechanical pencils, reading up on the history of these pencils, and appreciating its uses in daily life.

In Japan, some students view mechanical pencils as lucky tools, particularly during exam season.

Certain pencil designs are imbued with symbols or colors believed to bring success.

For example, red pencils are popular for marking correct answers and encouraging positivity.

Mechanical pencils are prized by artists for their precision. Manga illustrators in Japan often use fine mechanical pencil leads for initial sketches.

Similarly, architects and graphic designers rely on mechanical pencils for intricate designs and layouts.

The largest functional mechanical pencil was created in Malaysia. It measured over 19 feet long and used a custom lead mechanism. The pencil was part of an art installation to celebrate stationery tools.

Yes, some mechanical pencils are made from unexpected materials like bamboo or titanium.

Bamboo pencils are eco-friendly and lightweight, while titanium models appeal to those seeking durability. These designs highlight creativity in everyday tools.

Yes, lead thickness preferences vary worldwide. In Japan, thin leads (0.3mm) are popular for detailed writing, especially kanji characters.

In the U.S., 0.5mm and 0.7mm are more common for general use, reflecting regional handwriting styles.

The mechanism inside mechanical pencils is an example of simple yet effective engineering.

Push-button designs distribute lead evenly without sharpening. Some models, like the Uni Kuru Toga, even rotate the lead as you write, maintaining a sharp point.

High-end mechanical pencils exist, crafted by brands like Montblanc and Graf von Faber-Castell.

These models feature materials like gold, platinum, or rare woods. They’re popular among collectors and professionals who value craftsmanship.

A common myth is that mechanical pencils don’t last long. However, with proper care, they can endure for decades. Another misconception is that they’re entirely modern, though their origins date back to the 1820s.

Certain mechanical pencils are built to withstand extreme conditions. Space-grade models can work in zero gravity, while others are designed for cold environments.

These adaptations make them versatile tools for adventurers and professionals.

Some people use mechanical pencils for crafting, such as carving miniature sculptures from the lead.

Others repurpose them as styluses for touchscreen devices. These unconventional uses highlight their versatility.

When Rachel Maniscalco was placed on unpaid leave from her teaching job at Concord High School on Staten Island in October 2021, she almost lost everything along with it. Her husband earned too much money working at JFK International Airport to qualify for food stamps but not enough to support the whole family. The bills quickly started piling up: the mortgage, utilities, car insurance. And because Maniscalco’s older daughter had medical issues, the family had to start paying $600 a month for private health insurance. Maniscalco drained her retirement savings; her husband drained his savings.

To try and make ends meet, Maniscalco started working at a tax office and picking up night shifts at a bar, along with other side gigs—anything to patch together an income. One hundred dollars from the bar would be enough to cover a few weeknight dinners; a fifty-dollar tutoring session would buy two cans of formula for her newborn. Between all the odd jobs, Maniscalco barely got any sleep. “I was running on fumes for years,” she told me. Still, it wasn’t enough: “Things are going to be scarce . . . for a little bit,” she recalls telling her daughter.

Why did Maniscalco—a special education and English teacher in New York City public schools for over a decade—lose her job? She was one of the thousands of educators, police officers, sanitation workers, and other city employees who refused to get the Covid-19 vaccine. Maniscalco didn’t know this when she first lost her job, but she would help start a movement that would unite thousands of aggrieved citizens in opposition to New York’s immunization requirements for public workers. The “reinstate and compensate” movement, as it is sometimes referred to by its devotees, is a microcosm of the libertarian approach to public health that has been galvanized nationwide since the pandemic.

Though New York City eventually jettisoned its mandate and allowed most unvaccinated workers to return to their jobs, Maniscalco and many others like her are not back at work—they’re still fighting for the cause of “medical freedom.” Indeed, they’ve been welcomed with open arms into the Make America Healthy Again coalition against government authority and elite expertise in most every form, public health be damned.

Before Covid, Maniscalco never cared much about politics. “I lived my life very focused on how I’m getting through . . . the next paycheck cycle,” she told me. But then normal life ground to a halt: In March 2020, Maniscalco and her family were suddenly stuck together in the house all day. Maniscalco sat at the dining room table every morning and tried to work with her students over Zoom—but it was a struggle. Her daughter, who was in the third grade at the time, likewise had trouble with remote learning. “I mean, who wouldn’t, really, right? . . . It was just an absolute nightmare.” As the pandemic wore on, Maniscalco grew tired of all the rules, the fear, the doom and gloom. She wanted to focus on the bright side: the doctors who projected that we had a high chance—99.7 percent, as she recalls—of getting through the pandemic. The ones who said you would be just fine as long as you weren’t morbidly obese, old, or had any other comorbidities. That the danger of Covid-19 was wildly overblown.

The reinstate-and-compensate movement “spread like wildfire” through word of mouth and social media.

One of these “doctors” is the decertified Peter McCullough, an early proponent of antiparasitic medications like ivermectin and chloroquine as treatments for Covid-19. McCullough also pushed the narrative that Covid-19 survivors had immunity and didn’t need to be vaccinated: “People who develop Covid have complete and durable immunity,” he said in his testimony to the Texas Senate Health and Human Services Committee. “There is no scientific, clinical, or safety rationale for ever vaccinating a Covid-recovered patient.” His ideas were circulated by manosphere conspiracists like Joe Rogan, who parroted McCullough’s unsubstantiated claims to millions, even alleging he had treated himself with ivermectin.

Maniscalco, along with millions of others, was swept up in this cataclysmic information battle that politicized what, for most, was a public health emergency requiring a nonpartisan response. As she researched further, Maniscalco grew increasingly skeptical of the vaccine, which became widely available to New Yorkers in April 2021. “I read one study from the New England Journal of Medicine that said that [the vaccine] was not definitively safe for pregnant women,” she told me. She appeared to be referring to a study published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in April 2021, which concluded that “preliminary findings did not show obvious safety signals among pregnant persons who received mRNA Covid-19 vaccines.” The term “safety signal” is pharmaceutical regulation jargon for “information on a new or known adverse event that is potentially caused by a medicine and that warrants further investigation,” meaning that, in actuality, the CDC’s conclusion was that there was no evidence of unexpected safety problems for pregnant people in its preliminary trial.

Maniscalco came to believe that the vaccine was foisted onto the public to generate profits for its manufacturers. “If you look at it from a financial perspective, people made so much money off of this experimental pharmaceutical,” she contended. “Big Pharma controls so much—including the media, by the way, all of the media—that the only thing that made sense to me was that the kickbacks were so monumental that no one could go against this Goliath.”

The conviction that federal agencies bolster pharmaceutical companies’ profits is, of course, not without a basis in reality. Between 2014 and 2018, the CDC accepted close to $80 million from drug companies and other corporations through its charitable foundation. The federal government, in turn, poured approximately $18 billion into accelerating vaccine research and development through Operation Warp Speed. But despite taxpayers already bankrolling much of the vaccine effort, the U.S. government paid Pfizer about $1.95 billion for the first 100 million doses and later paid Moderna about $3.3 billion for an additional 200 million doses. In 2022—just one year after governments around the world began distributing Covid vaccines—Pfizer’s revenue hit $100 billion, a new record. A few months later, both Pfizer and Moderna quadrupled the price of their vaccines.

In August 2021, Maniscalco learned that New York City would require her to receive at least one dose of the vaccine to return to in-person work—or else be placed on unpaid leave. She knew she wasn’t going to comply. She had just had her second daughter in June at thirty-six years old, and the fear of any possible complications about having a baby at her age led her to increased skepticism about the vaccine. She decided that she would not put “anything in my body that may lead to a negative outcome.” Other employees told me they refused the vaccine due to their religious beliefs. One former public school social worker told me she did not get the vaccine because she is a pro-life Catholic and had read that the vaccine was created using “abortion cells.” But since 2019, New York has been one of only five states that do not allow religious or personal exemptions from school vaccine requirements.

On October 4, the first day of school after the mandates took effect, Maniscalco was one of eight thousand employees who were unable to work because they refused the vaccine. And that was just the Department of Education. A month later, another nine thousand employees from the fire, police, and sanitation departments were placed on unpaid leave.

It was around that time that Maniscalco started a new Instagram account dedicated to protesting the vaccine mandate. One of Maniscalco’s first posts is a video of her standing at a microphone at a protest in Manhattan. Her hair is in a ponytail, and her newborn bounces in her arms as her voice reverberates through the industrial speakers. She tells the assembled crowd that she’s been reaching out to the teachers’ union, asking it to support their decision not to get vaccinated, but that it had not responded. She says that PCR tests are “bullshit” and that the powers that be “don’t care about medical freedom and bodily autonomy.” (Today, the account boasts around seventeen thousand followers.)

According to Maniscalco, the reinstate and compensate movement “spread like wildfire” through word of mouth and social media. That’s how she met Michael Kane, a former high school teacher in Queens who shared her grievances and her outspokenness. After the mandate was announced, Kane established Teachers for Choice, an organization that shares vaccine-related news and updates at the federal and state levels. Its ethos is simple: As Kane put it on his Substack, the movement opposes all “forced medical mandates for any American to access society or keep their job.”

Kane and Maniscalco ramped up their efforts to lobby the teachers’ union to stand up to NYC Public Schools (NYCPS), then known as the NYC Department of Education, on their behalf. The United Federation of Teachers (UFT) was generally supportive of vaccination programs for teachers in New York City, but it did make some effort to advocate for the anti-vaccination teachers. The UFT negotiated for teachers with medical exemptions to teach remotely, health benefits for teachers placed on leave, and severance options for those who would not comply. Nevertheless, in August 2021, Kane posted a press release to announce he was leaving the union. “The UFT is no longer a union. What union in history has ever actively worked to have their members placed on unpaid leave or fired?” Kane wrote on his Substack. “This is one of the saddest days of my life.”

David C. Bloomfield, a professor of education law at Brooklyn College and the CUNY Graduate Center, is sympathetic to the position the UFT took during the pandemic. “The UFT had members who may have wanted [to be] protected from other members,” he mused. “So, I think the UFT was put in a spot.” A spokesperson for the UFT said that the union worked with NYCPS to help its members seek religious and medical exemptions. Maniscalco remembers it differently: “Our union, who I paid dues to for a decade, did absolutely nothing for us. . . . You go against what they want, what the city wants, what the union wants, what the union signs up for, [and] they will fuck you every which way.”

Of the over sixteen thousand municipal employees who were placed on unpaid leave around the time the mandate went into effect, most caved within a few days. By November 10, 2021, only 2,600 New York City employees remained on unpaid leave. By 2022, the city started firing the holdouts. Maniscalco and Kane were two of nearly 1,000 NYCPS employees and over 1,700 municipal employees who were terminated during these sweeping layoffs.

Maniscalco, Kane, and hundreds of other fired workers subsequently turned to the courts. Maniscalco hired a lawyer. Jimmy Wagner—whose wife was also a teacher wary of the vaccine at the time—took on her case and several other tenured teachers’ cases pro bono at first. Wagner argues that Maniscalco’s firing was not only unjustified but also illegal because she had tenure. A teacher seeking tenure with NYCPS must complete a four-year probationary period, receive a recommendation from their principal, and have a clean record. If the superintendent grants tenure, the teacher cannot be fired without due process and is entitled to a hearing should NYCPS pursue disciplinary action. “If Rachel Maniscalco had slapped a child . . . she would never have been fired,” Wagner insists.

According to him, New York’s tenure law should have superseded the city’s collective bargaining agreement with the teachers’ union requiring vaccines. He wasn’t arguing that teachers could not be fired—just that they had a right to a hearing and due process, which Maniscalco was denied. Wagner and Maniscalco brought their case to the Supreme Court of New York in March 2022 and again in February 2023. Both times, they lost.

For its part, NYCPS argued that due process was not violated because their placement on leave was “unrelated to job performance, misconduct or competency” and therefore didn’t count as disciplinary action. “Tenure protections aren’t built for the situation that the city found itself in in 2020,” said Dr. Bloomfield. He allows that the tenure statute in New York education law is “procedurally complex and drawn-out,” but even so, he remains “dubious about its applicability in this situation.”

And then a funny thing happened: In February 2023, New York City lifted the vaccine mandate for municipal workers. But within the NYCPS, fired employees were not immediately reinstated to their posts; they had to reapply for them. During this process, many, including Maniscalco, discovered that their personnel files had been flagged with “problem codes,” delaying their background checks. Maniscalco, Kane, and a group of others testified in a city council hearing in December 2023 to have these removed—to no avail.

In the years since, Maniscalco, Kane, and other rising figures in the anti-vaccination space have pressed ahead, testifying at city council hearings, appearing in court proceedings, and lobbying politicians. In February 2025, Maniscalco and her lawyer founded a new political organization: the Donald J. Trump Kings County Republican Club. Originally, it was dedicated to electing local politicians whose politics aligned with the reinstate and compensate movement, but after disappointing results in that year’s election, the club pivoted to reforming the city charter.

The first two proposed changes are to allow elected officials to be recalled and to create an elected Office of Municipal Worker Fairness. From Wagner’s point of view, this is all about freedom: the ever-contentious, all-important American right to choose. “For the last sixty years, all women in New York State have heard is ‘my body, my choice.’ How, in the blink of an eye, [do] they go from ‘my body, my choice’ to the government’s choice?”

Maniscalco and Wagner now insist that their movement is ultimately about workers’ rights.

While Wagner, Maniscalco, and other vocal advocates of the “reinstate and compensate” movement have stressed to me time and time again that they are not MAGA acolytes, they are animated by hostility to the Democratic Party, which they see as responsible for the economic hardship they have endured in recent years. Bill de Blasio created the mandate, but it was during the Eric Adams administration that NYCPS employees were officially terminated en masse. In the eyes of fired workers, Adams had not only ignored their grievances but underscored them when, in the spring of 2022, he lifted the vaccine mandate for athletes and performers but not city workers. By the time the mandate for city workers was finally lifted a year later, it was seen by many as too little, too late.

On the morning of November 5, 2025—less than twenty-four hours after Zohran Mamdani won the mayoral election—the lame-duck Adams administration announced that the city’s administrative department, the Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS), would hold a public hearing for the proposed “Reinstatement of Employees Dismissed for Noncompliance with the COVID-19 Vaccination Mandate.” If approved, this rule would have allowed 2,900 former city workers to reapply for their old titles at their former salaries—but without backpay. Despite a flurry of excitement at the end of the year, the proposal was never voted on and was lost in a bureaucratic abyss. (DCAS did not respond to multiple requests for comment.)

When Mamdani stepped into the mayor’s office on January 1, I assumed that Maniscalco and her fellow activists would be enraged by the election of a self-proclaimed socialist—after all, I had heard them decry the city’s progressives as “violent oligarchs” and the “radical left” more than once. But when asked about the new administration, Maniscalco appeared wary, but not close-minded. Throughout his campaign, Mamdani centered his platform around making life in New York City easier for the working class. But what remains to be seen, in Maniscalco’s eyes, is whether his pro-worker ethos will extend across ideological lines. “Is it every worker,” she wonders, “or the people you agree with?”

Last March on the campaign trail, movement organizers reported that Mamdani “seemed genuinely interested” when they handed him a flyer outlining their grievances. Allegedly, he told them that he did not want them to “fall through the cracks.” But about a month later, Mamdani backtracked while speaking with former New York Police Department lieutenant John Macari on his podcast New York’s Finest: Retired and Unfiltered. A listener and NYPD officer named Marlon, who was fired for refusing the vaccine, submitted a question: If elected mayor, would Mamdani hire him back to the force? Mamdani sympathized with Marlon and acknowledged that some of the city’s pandemic-era rules had been arbitrary. But he also stressed the importance of following public health guidance during an emergency like the pandemic. “Ultimately, if you asked me today, would I be hiring Marlon back? I think I would fall on the side of no because of the concerns around the necessity of upholding that public health mandate.” (The mayor’s office did not respond to a request for comment.)

On a freezing Tuesday morning this past March, Maniscalco and other reinstate and compensate activists woke up at the crack of dawn to take a bus to the New York State Capitol in Albany for “Vaccine Rights Advocacy Day”— an annual rally in Empire State Plaza. At the rally, people held up homemade signs plastered with Health and Human Services Secretary John Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.’s smiling face and messages like “COERCION ≠ CONSENT.” Michael Kane was the event’s emcee. As he stepped into the center of the crowd, he began a chant: “Hands off our children.” Behind him, a three-drum, one-trombone band accompanied the crowd’s fervent cheers.

Someone gave me a flyer that was printed on both sides with horrifying statistics like “40 percent of all kids have a vaccine-induced chronic illness” (presumably, this came from the White House’s 2025 MAHA Report, which lists the percentage but never attributes it to vaccines). There were screenshots of blurry tables and graphs from medical studies (cited but easily discredited after even a cursory skim of authoritative sources). At the bottom of the page, Children’s Health Defense’s website was printed in big, bold lettering.

CHD—a nonprofit organization founded in 2007 by Eric Gladen as the World Mercury Project—was the main sponsor of the rally; its banner hung behind Kane as he spoke (Kane also recently became CHD’s Director of Advocacy). Children’s Health Defense is a MAHA-backed nonprofit that uses incessant litigation to advance legislation that rolls back vaccine requirements and other perceived threats to “medical freedom.” The group rose to prominence in 2015 when it appointed a new chairman and chief general counsel: Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. Appropriately, one of Children’s Health Defense’s central functions is to engage in endless litigation.

In New York City, CHD’s legal arm has represented several fired workers in wrongful termination lawsuits. Kane was represented by CHD attorney Sujata Gibson in his lawsuit against the city. Although Kane’s case was dismissed by the U.S. Supreme Court after five years of appeals and petitions, the Supreme Court also recently directed a lower court to review New York’s statewide ban on religious exemptions. CHD’s attorneys are persistent, and not without good reason. A couple of fired workers in the sanitation and fire departments achieved reinstatement through legal challenges and accommodation requests, and in October 2022, sixteen sanitation workers won reinstatement and back pay after a Staten Island court called the vaccine mandate itself arbitrary and capricious. Wagner himself told me that some of his clients had successfully sued for reinstatement and backpay. He told me he had “no theory” as to why Maniscalco’s lawsuits had failed while others hadn’t. “It’s the luck of the draw.”

CHD CEO Mary Holland was the final speaker at the Albany rally. She announced she and Gibson had filed a new suit against the state to restore religious exemptions from vaccination for children attending New York schools. This is just one of their several active lawsuits across the country, and they are not alone: in January, CHD and a dozen or so adjacent organizations announced they had signed on to the Medical Freedom Act Coalition, which has lobbied for state-level bills that loosen public health regulations and mandates. (The coalition’s motto is: “No one and no government has the right to mandate medical interventions.”) They have already successfully passed legislation in Idaho that “prevents schools, businesses, and day cares from mandating medical interventions” at all. In February, Iowa advanced a bill to eliminate school vaccine requirements entirely.

The coalition is working with at least four other states across the country to advance similar bills. As of this June, Florida’s campaign to end school vaccine mandates had stalled, while Arizona’s governor vetoed bills that would have banned mask mandates and loosened vaccine requirements. Still, dozens of anti-vaccine or exemption-expanding bills are active in legislatures across the country. The Trump administration is also pushing for reinstatements of laid off or fired workers at the federal level—in January 2025, Trump directed the Department of Defense to reinstate all service members dismissed for vaccine noncompliance. Since then, approximately two hundred troops and eighty-five Coast Guard members have been reinstated.

However, after a series of CDC and FDA decisions that seemed to favor vaccines, fired workers have started to wonder whether the Trump administration is truly on their side. The New York Times ran two feature stories in the spring about the fracturing of the MAHA–MAGA alliance. Although RFK, Jr.’s initial actions seemed promising, courts, Congress, and internal HHS pressure have reversed or stymied much of the MAHA agenda. Derrick Wynne, a MAHA adherent who was discharged from the Army for refusing a Covid vaccine, told the Times that he now believes Kennedy “was using our movement to gain a huge amount of traction.”

At this point, Maniscalco doesn’t even want her job back at NYCPS. “Could I go back and feel at peace? Could I feel safe? Never. I will never feel safe again there. Quite frankly, I don’t know that I’ll ever feel safe in a job again.” For her and other former government workers, the issue is now bigger than their own reinstatement: It’s become a righteous battle for justice. Indeed, Maniscalco and Wagner now insist that their movement is ultimately about workers’ rights. “That’s bipartisan,” Maniscalco told me.

The version of freedom they purport to defend conceives only of individual autonomy—and treats mutual obligation as akin to tyranny. But diseases do not care about our personal freedoms, political leanings, or whether we trust the powers that be. What we have learned through the pandemic is that when we live in community with others, the limits of our bodies do not start or end where they seem to; our bodies are not borders. Whether the vaccine mandates were punitive or arbitrary is no longer the essential question. The question is whether we can rebuild a public health system based on collective responsibility and trust before the next pandemic.
